ideas.plain_english: Add Apple Pay, Google Pay and PayPal buttons at the buy decision.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when wallet share of payments is meaningful and mobile traffic dominates.

ideas.title: Review detail: verified badge, photos, and reviewer context
ideas.hypothesis: If reviews carry a title, verified-buyer badge, reviewer photo or name, and customer photos of the product, then conversion rate will increase, because specific, attributable reviews are read as real while anonymous star counts are read as marketing.
ideas.run_when: A review platform is in place that can collect photos and verify purchases.
ideas.do_not_run_when: Reviews are thin or cannot be verified, since a 'verified' badge that is not earned is a trust liability.
ideas.plain_english: Show reviews with verified badges, photos and reviewer detail.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when a review platform can collect photos and verify purchases but currently shows bare stars.

ideas.title: Video testimonials on the product page
ideas.hypothesis: If short customer video testimonials are placed on the product page, then conversion rate will increase, because a real customer on camera is harder to discount than written text.
ideas.run_when: Genuine customer video exists and the product's benefit is demonstrable.
ideas.do_not_run_when: Only scripted or actor-led footage is available.
ideas.plain_english: Add short customer video testimonials to the product page.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when genuine customer video exists and the benefit is demonstrable on camera.

ideas.title: Quantity discount tiers with a recommended option
ideas.hypothesis: If quantity tiers are shown near the CTA with per-unit pricing and a labelled recommended or best-value option, then average order value will increase, because a labelled middle option reframes the decision from whether to buy to how many.
ideas.run_when: Product is consumable or repeat-use and margin supports volume pricing.
ideas.do_not_run_when: Product is a one-per-household durable, where multiples make no sense and the tiers read as a gimmick.
ideas.plain_english: Offer bulk pricing tiers with a recommended quantity.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when the product is consumable or repeat use and margin supports volume pricing.

ideas.title: Related and alternative product recommendations
ideas.hypothesis: If the product page shows 'shoppers also viewed' alternatives and complements below the buy decision, then revenue per visitor will increase, because a shopper who has rejected this specific product currently has no path except back or out.
ideas.run_when: Catalogue has genuine alternatives and product-page exit rate is high.
ideas.do_not_run_when: The block would sit above the buy decision and pull shoppers off a product they were about to buy.
ideas.plain_english: Show related and alternative products below the buy decision.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when the catalogue has genuine alternatives and product page exit rate is high.

ideas.title: Charity or give-back callout at the buy decision
ideas.hypothesis: If a specific give-back commitment is stated near the CTA, then conversion rate will increase, because a purchase that also does something is easier to justify at the moment of spending.
ideas.run_when: A genuine, specific and verifiable donation commitment exists.
ideas.do_not_run_when: The claim is vague or unverifiable, which reads as greenwashing and costs trust.
ideas.plain_english: State the specific give back commitment near the buy button.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run only where a genuine, specific and verifiable donation commitment exists.

ideas.title: Embedded social posts and message screenshots
ideas.hypothesis: If genuine social posts and message screenshots praising the product are embedded on the page, then conversion rate will increase, because unsolicited praise in a native format reads as unedited in a way an on-site testimonial does not.
ideas.run_when: Real posts exist and can be used with permission.
ideas.do_not_run_when: Screenshots would have to be recreated or staged.
ideas.plain_english: Embed genuine social posts and messages praising the product.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when real social posts praising the product exist and can be used with permission.

ideas.title: Buy button that skips the cart page
ideas.hypothesis: If the buy button sends the shopper straight to checkout (or a one-click upsell) instead of a cart page, then conversion rate will increase, because the cart page is a step that adds no information and offers an exit.
ideas.run_when: Single-product or single-item-order behaviour dominates and cart-to-checkout drop-off is material.
ideas.do_not_run_when: Multi-item baskets are the norm, or the cart page carries the free-shipping threshold and cross-sell that drive AOV.
ideas.plain_english: Send the buy button straight to checkout, skipping the cart page.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when single item orders dominate and cart to checkout drop off is material.

ideas.title: Cart and checkout details persist between visits
ideas.hypothesis: If cart contents and part-completed checkout fields persist when a shopper returns, then conversion rate will increase, because considered purchases span sessions and re-entry work is where returning intent dies.
ideas.run_when: Return-visit share is high and time-to-purchase spans more than one session.
ideas.do_not_run_when: Persistence would restore stale pricing or out-of-stock items without revalidation.
ideas.plain_english: Keep basket and checkout details saved between visits.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when return visit share is high and purchases typically span more than one session.

ideas.title: Inline validation and recoverable errors
ideas.hypothesis: If fields validate inline with clear pass and fail states, errors say exactly what to fix, and nothing already entered is lost on a failed submit, then conversion rate will increase, because a form error at the payment step is the most expensive moment to lose someone.
ideas.run_when: Checkout error events are frequent or replay shows repeated failed submits.
ideas.do_not_run_when: Validation fires so eagerly it marks fields wrong mid-typing.
ideas.plain_english: Validate fields as people type and keep what they entered on errors.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when checkout error events are frequent or replay shows repeated failed submits.

ideas.title: Clear order summary immediately before payment
ideas.hypothesis: If a full order summary (items, shipping, tax, total) is visible immediately before the pay button, then conversion rate will increase, because buyers will not commit to a total they cannot verify at the moment they press pay.
ideas.run_when: The summary is currently collapsed, on a prior step, or off-screen on mobile.
ideas.do_not_run_when: The summary already sits beside the pay button on every viewport.
ideas.plain_english: Show the full order total right before the pay button.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when the order summary is collapsed, on a prior step, or off screen on mobile.

ideas.title: Low-price order bumps at checkout
ideas.hypothesis: If checkout offers one or two cheap tick-box order bumps (priority handling, gift wrap, shipping protection), then average order value will increase, because a small add-on next to an already-committed total is a low-consideration decision.
ideas.run_when: The bump is genuinely useful, deliverable, and priced small relative to the order.
ideas.do_not_run_when: The bump would be pre-ticked, or it distracts from completing an already fragile checkout.
ideas.plain_english: Offer one or two cheap tick box extras at checkout.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when the add on is genuinely useful, deliverable and small relative to the order total.

ideas.title: Email captured as the first checkout field
ideas.hypothesis: If email is the first field in checkout, then revenue will increase, because abandoners become recoverable through abandoned-checkout flows instead of being lost entirely.
ideas.run_when: Abandoned-checkout email flows are live and checkout abandonment is material.
ideas.do_not_run_when: Asking for email first reads as a gate before the shopper can see shipping cost.
ideas.plain_english: Ask for the email address as the first checkout field.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when abandoned checkout email flows are live and checkout abandonment is material.

ideas.title: Never ask for the same information twice
ideas.hypothesis: If billing address defaults to the shipping address and no information is requested twice, then conversion rate will increase, because duplicate entry is pure cost at the point of payment.
ideas.run_when: Checkout currently asks for billing separately by default.
ideas.do_not_run_when: Payment or fraud rules genuinely require an independently entered billing address.
ideas.plain_english: Default billing address to shipping so nothing is typed twice.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when checkout asks for a billing address separately by default.

ideas.title: Address autocomplete and postcode lookup
ideas.hypothesis: If addresses are completed from a lookup and city or region auto-fills from the postcode, then conversion rate will increase, because the address block is the longest typing task in checkout and the one that most often fails on mobile.
ideas.run_when: Mobile share is high, address fields are long, and a lookup provider covers the shipping markets.
ideas.do_not_run_when: Coverage is poor in key markets, which traps buyers whose address the lookup cannot find.
ideas.plain_english: Autocomplete the address from a lookup or postcode.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when mobile share is high and a lookup provider covers the shipping markets.

ideas.title: Delivery date, courier and how to track
ideas.hypothesis: If the confirmation page states the expected arrival date, the courier and how to track the parcel, then revenue will increase, because post-purchase certainty reduces cancellations and support contacts and raises the odds of a second order.
ideas.run_when: Delivery estimates are accurate enough to publish and tracking is available.
ideas.do_not_run_when: Fulfilment times are unpredictable, where a stated date creates a promise that will be broken.
ideas.plain_english: State the delivery date, courier and how to track on confirmation.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when delivery estimates are accurate enough to publish and tracking is available.

ideas.title: Next-purchase coupon on the confirmation page
ideas.hypothesis: If the confirmation page issues a coupon for the next order (or one to pass to a friend), then revenue will increase, because the moment after purchase is the cheapest point at which to buy a second purchase.
ideas.run_when: Repeat purchase is a real behaviour in the category and margin supports the incentive.
ideas.do_not_run_when: Purchase is genuinely one-off, or the discount would train buyers to wait for codes.
ideas.plain_english: Give a discount code for the next order on the confirmation page.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when repeat purchase is real in the category and margin supports the incentive.

ideas.title: What the order confirmation email carries
ideas.hypothesis: If the confirmation email repeats the order summary, delivery expectations and any post-purchase offer or coupon shown on the thank-you page, then revenue will increase, because the confirmation email is the most-opened message the store ever sends and currently carries only a receipt.
ideas.run_when: Confirmation email is a bare transactional template and post-purchase offers exist.
ideas.do_not_run_when: Local rules restrict marketing content inside transactional messages.
ideas.plain_english: Add the order summary, delivery detail and next offer to the confirmation email.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when the confirmation email is a bare receipt and post purchase offers already exist.

ideas.title: Third-party review badge or rating widget (Trustpilot, Google)
ideas.hypothesis: If a third-party review platform badge with the live aggregate score is shown near the buying decision, then CVR increases, because proof the store cannot edit itself carries more weight than on-site testimonials for a first-time visitor.
ideas.run_when: The store has a genuine third-party rating at or above roughly the category norm, and survey or support evidence shows first-time buyers questioning legitimacy.
ideas.do_not_run_when: The third-party score is weak or thin, or on-site review widgets have already been tested and moved nothing (the badge is a smaller version of the same signal).
ideas.plain_english: Show the Trustpilot or Google rating near the buy decision.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when the store has a genuine third party rating at or above the category norm and buyers question legitimacy.

ideas.title: Two-card 'start here' entry path for first-time visitors
ideas.hypothesis: If the homepage offers two clearly labelled entry cards that split visitors by their obvious starting difference (new to the category vs knows what they want), then CVR increases, because visitors who do not know where to begin get a single named next step instead of a full catalogue.
ideas.run_when: Survey or session data shows visitors saying they do not know where to start, and the catalogue is broad enough that the homepage currently offers many equal-weight entry points.
ideas.do_not_run_when: The range is narrow enough that one product line carries most revenue, where the split just adds a click in front of the money page.
ideas.plain_english: Offer two clear starting paths for first time visitors.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when research shows visitors saying they do not know where to start and the homepage offers many equal entry points.

ideas.title: Return or satisfaction rate stated beside the guarantee
ideas.hypothesis: If the guarantee is stated with the actual return or satisfaction rate beside it, then CVR increases, because a specific number answers the doubt the guarantee itself creates (why would they need one) rather than leaving the reader to guess.
ideas.run_when: The store's return rate is genuinely low or its satisfaction rate genuinely high, and the number can be substantiated if a customer asks.
ideas.do_not_run_when: The rate is unflattering or cannot be verified from the order data, or the category makes returns normal enough that quoting a rate raises the topic for no gain.
ideas.plain_english: State the actual return or satisfaction rate beside the guarantee.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when the return rate is genuinely low or satisfaction genuinely high and the number can be substantiated.

ideas.title: Long-term promise backed by company track record
ideas.hypothesis: If a long-dated promise (lifetime warranty, spare parts availability, replacement cover) is stated together with concrete evidence the company will still be here to honour it, then CVR increases, because the promise only reduces risk once the buyer believes the company outlives it.
ideas.run_when: The product carries a long or lifetime warranty and the brand has a verifiable trading history, and reviews or support tickets show buyers questioning whether the cover is real.
ideas.do_not_run_when: The brand is young or the warranty is short, where raising the question of longevity introduces a doubt the buyer did not have.
ideas.plain_english: Back the long warranty with proof the company will still be here.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when the product carries a long warranty, the brand has trading history, and buyers question whether cover is real.

ideas.title: Credit the entry product's price against the full purchase
ideas.hypothesis: If buyers of a cheap entry product are told its price comes off the full-size or premium version later, then revenue per visitor increases, because the low-risk first purchase stops competing with the main one and becomes a step toward it.
ideas.run_when: There is a genuine entry product (sample, starter size, single unit) and a clear step up, and margin allows the credit.
ideas.do_not_run_when: The entry product is already the volume seller at healthy margin, where the credit cannibalises full-price purchases that would have happened anyway.
ideas.plain_english: Credit the price of the sample or starter size against the full product.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when a genuine entry product and a clear step up exist and margin allows the credit.

ideas.title: Key-spec summary table under the product title
ideas.hypothesis: If the four or five specs buyers actually ask about are put in a scannable table directly under the product title, then CVR increases, because the answers arrive before the buyer has to hunt through description copy or leave to check.
ideas.run_when: Support tickets, reviews or on-site search show the same handful of spec questions repeating, and those answers currently sit in body copy or a tab.
ideas.do_not_run_when: The product has few meaningful specs, or the table would simply restate the variant selector.
ideas.plain_english: Put the four or five key specs in a table under the title.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when support tickets, reviews or site search show the same handful of spec questions repeating.

ideas.title: Save this product and remind me later capture
ideas.hypothesis: If visitors who are interested but not ready can save the product and choose to be reminded (on a date, on a price drop, when it is back in stock), then captured demand and downstream revenue per visitor increase, because the 'not now for budget reasons' visitor currently leaves with no way back.
ideas.run_when: Research shows budget timing rather than doubt is a leading reason for not buying, and there is a working email or SMS trigger to fire the reminder.
ideas.do_not_run_when: The reminder cannot actually be sent, or the capture sits in the primary buying path where it competes with add-to-cart.
ideas.plain_english: Let shoppers save a product and be reminded later.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when research shows budget timing rather than doubt drives non purchase and a reminder trigger exists.

ideas.title: Exact price on cards instead of a 'from' price
ideas.hypothesis: If listing cards show the price the visitor will actually pay rather than a 'from' figure that rises on the product page, then CVR increases, because the first price seen matches the price at the decision and the visit does not carry a bait-and-switch impression into checkout.
ideas.run_when: Variant pricing means the 'from' figure understates what most buyers pay, and survey or review comments mention price surprise.
ideas.do_not_run_when: The spread across variants is wide and the entry price is a genuine and popular option, where showing the top price suppresses clicks into the range.
ideas.plain_english: Show the real price on cards instead of a from price.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when the from price understates what most buyers pay and comments mention price surprise.

ideas.title: Whole listing or category card clickable
ideas.hypothesis: If the entire card (image, title and surrounding tile) is a click target rather than just the title or image, then CVR increases, because dead clicks on the card body stop costing the visitor a retry and stop reading as a broken page.
ideas.run_when: Heatmaps or replay show dead clicks on card whitespace or imagery, particularly on mobile where the tap target is small.
ideas.do_not_run_when: The card carries its own secondary controls (quick add, colour swatches, wishlist) that a full-card link would swallow.
ideas.plain_english: Make the whole product card clickable, not just the title.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when heatmaps or replay show dead clicks on card whitespace, particularly on mobile.

ideas.title: Remove promo banners and popups from the buying path
ideas.hypothesis: If promo bars and interruptive popups are suppressed on the pages that already convert best, then CVR increases, because the CTA moves back into the first viewport and the visitor is not offered a detour to a weaker offer mid-decision.
ideas.run_when: Multiple promo layers stack above the fold, or an app-driven popup fires on the highest-converting template, and CTA visibility measurably suffers.
ideas.do_not_run_when: The banner carries information the offer depends on (a live sale, a shipping cut-off) with nowhere else to live.
ideas.plain_english: Remove promo bars and pop ups from the pages that convert best.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when promo layers stack above the fold or a pop up fires on the best converting template.

ideas.title: Remove site navigation from a dedicated offer page
ideas.hypothesis: If the header navigation is stripped from a paid-traffic offer page and replaced with on-page proof and FAQs, then CVR increases, because the only remaining paths are converting or leaving, and the questions the nav was used to answer are answered in place.
ideas.run_when: The page receives dedicated campaign traffic, exit analytics show visitors leaving via the header, and the page can carry its own proof and FAQ content.
ideas.do_not_run_when: The page also serves organic or returning traffic that needs the wider catalogue, or the offer is one of several the visitor should compare.
ideas.plain_english: Strip the menu from a dedicated offer page.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when a paid campaign page shows visitors exiting through the header and it can carry its own proof and FAQ.

ideas.title: Reviews filtered to the visitor's own segment
ideas.hypothesis: If the review block can be filtered to reviewers like the visitor (first-time buyer, use case, product variant), then CVR increases, because 'people like me managed it' answers the fit doubt that an averaged star rating does not.
ideas.run_when: Reviews carry structured attributes, volume is high enough that a filter still returns results, and the recurring objection is fit or difficulty rather than quality.
ideas.do_not_run_when: Review volume is thin, where filtering empties the block and reads worse than the unfiltered list.
ideas.plain_english: Let shoppers filter reviews to people like them.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when reviews carry structured attributes, volume is high, and the objection is fit or difficulty.

ideas.title: Offer shaped by what the customer already owns
ideas.hypothesis: If returning customers looking at a bundle are shown an offer that accounts for the items they already own, then revenue per visitor increases, because the repeat buyer stops feeling they are paying twice for the same thing.
ideas.run_when: Bundles or kits overlap heavily with items repeat customers already bought, and purchase history is available client-side or via the logged-in session.
ideas.do_not_run_when: Most traffic to the bundle is new customers, or the discount logic cannot be verified against real order history and would misprice.
ideas.plain_english: Adjust the bundle offer for items the customer already owns.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when bundles overlap with items repeat customers already bought and purchase history is available.

ideas.title: Three-tier good-better-best choice on the product page
ideas.hypothesis: If the product page presents the single item alongside a bundle and a premium tier in one three-column layout, then AOV increases, because the higher tier anchors the middle option and the upgrade is priced in view rather than discovered on another page.
ideas.run_when: A genuine ladder exists (single, kit, premium kit), the tiers differ on something the buyer cares about, and the top tier can carry the anchor without looking absurd.
ideas.do_not_run_when: The tiers differ only on quantity, or the extra columns push the primary CTA below the fold on mobile.
ideas.plain_english: Show single, bundle and premium options side by side.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when a genuine good, better, best ladder exists and tiers differ on something buyers care about.

ideas.title: Time-on-page triggered offer popup
ideas.hypothesis: If a discount is offered by popup after a visitor has spent a set time on a product page, then revenue per visitor increases, because the offer reaches the hesitating visitor at the point of stall rather than only at exit, though it also discounts buyers who would have paid full price.
ideas.run_when: Time-on-page distribution shows a clear stall point, margin absorbs the discount, and the offer size is set separately for cheap and expensive lines.
ideas.do_not_run_when: Exit-intent already carries an offer (the two cannibalise), or the site trains visitors to wait for a popup on every visit.
ideas.plain_english: Offer a discount by pop up after someone lingers on a product.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when time on page shows a clear stall point and margin absorbs the discount.

ideas.title: Complementary product offer inside the cart
ideas.hypothesis: If the cart shows one relevant complementary item that can be added in place, then AOV increases, because the visitor is committed to buying and the add costs one tap without leaving the cart, while a suppression rule stops recommending what is already in the basket.
ideas.run_when: Order data shows a repeatable pairing, and the cart or drawer has room for one add without pushing checkout below the fold.
ideas.do_not_run_when: The cart is already a friction point with a weak begin-checkout rate, where anything added between the basket and the pay button costs more than it earns.
ideas.plain_english: Offer one matching add on product inside the cart.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when order data shows a repeatable pairing and the cart has room without pushing checkout down.

ideas.title: Price-match or best-price guarantee near the CTA
ideas.hypothesis: If the product page promises to match or refund the difference on a better price found within a set window, then CVR increases, because the buyer stops leaving to hunt for a coupon or a cheaper stockist before committing.
ideas.run_when: The category is discount-heavy or coupon-hunting shows up in exit behaviour, and the business can honour the claim without eroding margin badly.
ideas.do_not_run_when: The store runs frequent sitewide sales of its own, where the promise mostly triggers refunds on purchases already made.
ideas.plain_english: Promise to match or refund the difference on a better price.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when the category is discount heavy or coupon hunting shows in exit behaviour and margin can absorb it.

ideas.title: Recent-purchase notifications on the buying path
ideas.hypothesis: If small notifications show genuine recent orders while the visitor is on the product page, then CVR increases, because live purchase activity signals other people are buying now, though the same widget is a well-known trust liability when it reads as fake.
ideas.run_when: Order frequency is high enough that the notifications are real and recent, and the store has no existing scepticism problem in reviews or survey comments.
ideas.do_not_run_when: Order volume is low (the widget will repeat or invent), or research already shows visitors calling the site scammy, where this compounds it. Treat as a candidate loss.
ideas.plain_english: Show small pop ups of other people's recent orders.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run only when order frequency makes notifications genuinely real and reviews show no scepticism problem.

ideas.title: Named expert or maker credentials beside the product
ideas.hypothesis: If the people behind the product are shown with specific credentials rather than a generic brand story, then CVR increases, because a named person with verifiable experience is a stronger competence signal than the company voice for a first-time buyer.
ideas.run_when: The product's value depends on expertise (engineered, formulated, hand-made) and there is a real person with credentials worth naming.
ideas.do_not_run_when: The credentials are vague or the section pushes proof the buyer actually wants (reviews, specs) further down the page.
ideas.plain_english: Name the expert or maker behind the product with their credentials.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when the product's value depends on expertise and a real person with credentials can be named.

ideas.title: Visual 'what you get' laydown of everything included
ideas.hypothesis: If everything included is shown as one laid-out image rather than listed as text, then CVR increases, because a bundle read as a picture registers as more substantial than the same contents read as bullets, and buyers stop wondering what physically arrives.
ideas.run_when: The product is a kit, bundle or multi-part item, and support questions or reviews show confusion about what is included.
ideas.do_not_run_when: The item is a single obvious object, where the laydown adds a gallery slide with nothing to say.
ideas.plain_english: Show everything included as one laid out photo.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when the product is a kit or bundle and support questions show confusion about what is included.

ideas.title: Proof aimed at the single biggest stated objection, placed at the decision point
ideas.hypothesis: If a specific quantified stat or customer quote answering the top research-identified objection is placed where that objection is felt, then CVR increases, because generic proof does not touch the reason non-buyers give for leaving.
ideas.run_when: Survey or review research names one dominant objection and there is an honest, quantified line that answers it.
ideas.do_not_run_when: The stat cannot be verified, or the objection is a distant third or lower in the research.
ideas.plain_english: Answer the single biggest objection right where it is felt.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when survey or review research names one dominant objection and an honest quantified answer exists.

ideas.title: Full homepage concept redesign
ideas.hypothesis: If the homepage is rebuilt around orientation and value proposition rather than lifestyle imagery, then CVR increases, because an inconclusive first attempt showed the page moves but the previous swing over-corrected on a single axis.
ideas.run_when: A prior homepage change moved metrics without a clean read and traffic is high enough to power a multi-element change.
ideas.do_not_run_when: Single-element homepage tests are still unexhausted, or the redesign confounds messaging with layout so the winner cannot be attributed.
ideas.plain_english: Rebuild the homepage around orientation and value proposition.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run only when single element homepage tests are exhausted and traffic can power a multi element change.

ideas.title: Notify-me-of-a-sale email capture
ideas.hypothesis: If visitors can ask to be told when the product goes on sale, then lead rate increases, because a large slice of non-purchasers say they are simply waiting for a discount and currently leave with no way back.
ideas.run_when: Exit research shows a meaningful share of non-buyers are price-waiting and the brand does run periodic promotions.
ideas.do_not_run_when: The brand never discounts, or the capture would train full-price buyers to wait.
ideas.plain_english: Let visitors ask to be told when the product goes on sale.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when exit research shows a meaningful share of non buyers are waiting for a discount and the brand does promote.

ideas.title: Merchandised products inside the navigation menu
ideas.hypothesis: If best sellers, product imagery or a most-popular badge appear inside the menu, then CVR increases among nav users, because a text-only menu makes the visitor choose before they have seen anything.
ideas.run_when: Nav touch rate is high enough to read on an exposure-segmented population, and prior structural nav changes failed on abstraction rather than on placement.
ideas.do_not_run_when: Nav touch rate is a few percent of sessions and the test will be read sitewide, or another nav test is live on the same menu.
ideas.plain_english: Put best sellers and product images inside the navigation menu.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when nav touch rate is high enough to read on an exposure segmented population.

ideas.title: Customer or demo video section showing the product in use
ideas.hypothesis: If a see-it-in-action video section is added to the product page, then CVR increases, because seeing the product used is the most-cited tipping point in buyer research.
ideas.run_when: Research names video or seeing it in person as the top purchase trigger and usable footage exists.
ideas.do_not_run_when: The video asset adds enough page weight to offset the gain, or a video widget on the same template has already been shown to cost RPV.
ideas.plain_english: Add a section showing the product being used on video.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when research names seeing it in action as the top purchase trigger and usable footage exists.

ideas.title: Payment method icons before checkout
ideas.hypothesis: If accepted payment methods are shown near the add-to-cart or in the cart drawer, then checkout begin rate increases, because visitors in markets with strong local payment habits do not know their method is accepted until they are already deep in checkout.
ideas.run_when: A market shows a large checkout completion gap and local payment methods are genuinely enabled.
ideas.do_not_run_when: The icons would advertise methods that are not actually available, or the same test already read inconclusive on this template in a market with no payment-method concern.
ideas.plain_english: Show the accepted payment logos before checkout.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when a market shows a checkout completion gap and local payment methods are genuinely enabled.

ideas.title: Exit-intent email capture modal
ideas.hypothesis: If a capture modal fires on exit intent, then lead rate increases, because leaving visitors are otherwise lost with no retargetable identity.
ideas.run_when: Desktop exit volume is high and no exit-triggered capture exists.
ideas.do_not_run_when: Other popups already compete on the same page, or the modal would fire over an active buy decision.
ideas.plain_english: Show an email capture pop up as visitors go to leave.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when desktop exit volume is high and no exit triggered capture exists.

ideas.title: Shipping cost or shipping offer made visible before add-to-cart
ideas.hypothesis: If the shipping cost, flat rate or free-shipping progress is shown on the product page rather than first appearing in checkout, then CVR increases, because shipping is a top stated barrier and discovering it late reads as a surprise charge.
ideas.run_when: Shipping is named as a major barrier in exit research, or the offer is visible on one device and invisible on the other.
ideas.do_not_run_when: The shipping cost is high enough that surfacing it early kills add-to-cart, or prior shipping-offer tests in the market have been negative.
ideas.plain_english: Show the shipping cost or offer before add to cart.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when shipping is named as a major barrier in exit research or the offer shows on one device only.

ideas.title: Benefit-led product headline and subheading
ideas.hypothesis: If the product headline and subheading state the outcome rather than the product name, then CVR increases, because pages whose fold says nothing about the benefit bounce well above the category norm.
ideas.run_when: Bounce on the product template is materially above a comparable template, and research shows visitors cannot tell what the product does for them.
ideas.do_not_run_when: The change is bundled with a hero redesign so copy and design cannot be separated.
ideas.plain_english: Rewrite the product headline to state the outcome, not the name.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when bounce on the product template is well above a comparable template and visitors cannot tell what it does.

ideas.title: State what a promo code actually applies to, where it is offered
ideas.hypothesis: If the promo popup and product page state which products the code covers, then CVR increases, because customers who assume a sitewide discount and then find it rejected at the cart read the offer as a bait and switch and abandon.
ideas.run_when: Post-purchase or checkout surveys surface complaints about a code not applying.
ideas.do_not_run_when: The code genuinely does apply sitewide, or the clarity line would be so heavily caveated it kills the opt-in.
ideas.plain_english: Say which products the promo code actually covers.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when post purchase or checkout surveys surface complaints about a code not applying.

ideas.title: Enable the market's native payment methods at checkout
ideas.hypothesis: If the payment methods people in a market actually use are enabled at checkout, then checkout completion increases, because a card-only checkout asks customers in bank-transfer markets to pay in a way they do not normally pay.
ideas.run_when: A regional checkout completion gap coincides with markets that have dominant local payment rails.
ideas.do_not_run_when: The gap is explained by shipping cost or language rather than payment, or the methods cannot be enabled by the finance owner.
ideas.plain_english: Enable the payment methods people in that market actually use.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when a regional checkout completion gap coincides with markets that have dominant local payment rails.

ideas.title: Checkout in the customer's own language
ideas.hypothesis: If checkout is served in the visitor's browser language, whether by full translation, a switcher, or translating only the highest-friction fields, then checkout completion increases, because non-English speakers are being asked to enter an address and payment details in a language they did not choose.
ideas.run_when: Session replay of non-English-language visitors shows translate behaviour, address-field pauses or rage clicks at the payment step.
ideas.do_not_run_when: The replay evidence is absent, since full localisation is expensive to build and cheap to assume.
ideas.plain_english: Serve checkout in the visitor's own language.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when replay of non English visitors shows translation behaviour or pauses at the payment step.

ideas.title: "Free" label on payment methods that carry no surcharge
ideas.hypothesis: If each payment method at checkout is labelled 'free' in a contrasting colour, then orders will increase, because shoppers who expect a card or gateway surcharge stall at the payment step, and stating the zero fee at the moment of choice removes that expected cost before it is priced into the decision.
ideas.run_when: Checkout payment step where no payment method actually carries an additional charge, in markets where surcharging is common enough that shoppers expect it (NL/EU, AU), and where analytics or session replay shows drop-off at payment-method selection.
ideas.do_not_run_when: Any payment method genuinely carries a fee, the surcharge is shown later in the flow, or the checkout is a hosted third-party page where the label cannot be applied consistently to every method.
ideas.plain_english: Label each payment method as free where no fee applies.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run in markets where surcharges are common and replay shows drop off at payment method selection.

ideas.title: Remove oversized editorial or featured tiles that interrupt the product grid
ideas.hypothesis: If oversized featured or editorial tiles are removed so the collection page runs as one uninterrupted product grid, then revenue per visitor will increase, because SmartWool's mixed four-products-plus-one-featured layout lost to a conventional grid by 17.1% revenue per user at 95% confidence over 25,000+ visitors.
ideas.run_when: The collection grid is repeatedly broken by promotional or editorial tiles that occupy the space of multiple products, the SKUs are visually comparable, and shoppers need to scan many products to choose.
ideas.do_not_run_when: The catalogue is small enough to see in one screen, or the editorial blocks carry decision-critical information the product cards do not.
ideas.plain_english: Remove big editorial tiles so the product grid runs uninterrupted.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when oversized editorial tiles repeatedly break a grid of visually comparable products.

ideas.title: Dynamic unit-savings labels on larger sizes, packs and quantities
ideas.hypothesis: If each size, pack or subscription option carries a dynamically calculated saving (percent per unit or amount saved) that updates with the chosen configuration, then revenue per visitor will increase, because Stone Creek Coffee's dynamic per-ounce savings variant reached significance at +41% conversion rate and +26% revenue per visitor.
ideas.run_when: Larger sizes, multipacks or subscriptions genuinely have better unit economics, and the PDP currently lists options without translating the economics for the shopper. Consumables, coffee, supplements, pet, beauty replenishment and household categories.
ideas.do_not_run_when: There is no real per-unit saving to state, margin cannot absorb a mix shift into the discounted option, or AOV is the metric the business is protecting (Stone Creek's winner cut AOV 10% by shifting mix to subscription).
ideas.plain_english: Show the per unit saving on each size, pack or subscription option.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when larger sizes or packs genuinely have better unit economics and the page never states them.

ideas.title: Upgrade a one-off cart item to a subscription from the cart or side cart
ideas.hypothesis: If the cart offers a one-click upgrade of an existing one-off line item to a subscription with the saving stated, then subscription revenue will increase, because SiO Beauty's side-cart 'upgrade to subscription and save 10%' control reported a 16.5% increase in subscription revenue.
ideas.run_when: The catalogue is consumable and replenished, subscription economics are proven, and subscribe-and-save is currently only offered on the PDP where the decision competes with product selection.
ideas.do_not_run_when: Subscription retention or first-order margin is unproven, or the discount cost of the upgrade is not covered by measured LTV. Never judge this on subscription revenue alone: track total checkout CVR, immediate RPV, take rate, discount cost and churn alongside it.
ideas.plain_english: Let shoppers upgrade a cart item to a subscription in one click.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when the catalogue is replenished, subscription economics are proven, and subscribe and save is only on the product page.

ideas.title: Sticky filter and sort bar on the mobile collection page
ideas.hypothesis: If the mobile filter and sort controls stay pinned as the shopper scrolls the collection, then conversion rate will increase, because filtering narrows a long list to relevant products faster. Prior evidence contradicts this: Little Bible Stories lifted filter and sort interaction 299.58% while CVR fell 2.23% and RPV fell 1.8%.
ideas.run_when: Collections are long, filters map to real buying attributes, and analytics show filter users convert materially above average while filter usage is low because the control is scrolled out of view.
ideas.do_not_run_when: Filter engagement is the metric being sold as the win. Interaction with the control changed is not a success metric unless that interaction itself has business value. Size this test on CVR or RPV, not on filter clicks.
ideas.plain_english: Keep the mobile filter and sort buttons pinned while scrolling.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run only when filter users convert well above average and the control is scrolled out of view; size on CVR, never filter clicks.

ideas.title: Rewrite funnel step copy in the brand's conversational voice
ideas.hypothesis: If the copy on the early funnel steps is rewritten in the light, conversational brand voice used in acquisition creative instead of a formal transactional tone, then conversion to purchase will increase, because visitors arriving from brand-voice-heavy ads meet a consistent voice and read the step as part of the same brand experience rather than a generic form.
ideas.run_when: The brand has a distinctive, well-known voice in its ads and content, but the funnel or checkout copy was written separately and reads formally. Cheap to build, so worth running where funnel traffic is high.
ideas.do_not_run_when: The brand voice is neutral or the funnel copy already matches it, or the step carries legal/compliance wording that cannot be loosened.
ideas.plain_english: Rewrite the funnel copy in the brand's normal conversational voice.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when the brand has a distinctive voice in its ads but the funnel copy reads formally.

ideas.title: Break a bundle into its individual items with an itemised contents list
ideas.hypothesis: If a bundled offer is presented as its separate component products with a bullet-point list of what is included, then conversion will increase, because buyers can see and price each item rather than having to accept an opaque package, which removes the need to leave the page to work out what the bundle contains.
ideas.run_when: Session replay or analytics show pogosticking between the bundle page and individual product pages, or support/survey data shows buyers asking what is in the bundle.
ideas.do_not_run_when: The bundle is the margin play and the individual items are not separately sellable, or debundling would expose a per-item price that makes the bundle look poor value.
ideas.plain_english: Show the bundle as its separate items with a contents list.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when replay shows hopping between bundle and product pages, or buyers ask what is in the bundle.

ideas.title: Frame the post-order add-on offer as the next step in the order process
ideas.hypothesis: If the confirmation message is shrunk and marked as a completed step and the add-on marketplace is presented as an explicit second step, then ancillary revenue per order will increase, because the buyer reads the order as unfinished rather than done and treats the add-on browse as part of completing it.
ideas.run_when: There is a genuine add-on catalogue that can still be attached to the order after checkout, and the confirmation page currently buries it below the fold.
ideas.do_not_run_when: The order cannot actually be amended after confirmation, or the confirmation details themselves are a known support driver and must stay prominent.
ideas.plain_english: Present the post order add ons as the next step in the order.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when a genuine add on catalogue can still attach to the order and the confirmation page buries it.

ideas.title: Build-your-own bundle tool instead of fixed preset bundles
ideas.hypothesis: If buyers can assemble their own bundle from the catalogue instead of choosing between fixed preset bundles, then average order value will increase, because the multi-item purchase stops depending on a preset happening to match what they want.
ideas.run_when: The catalogue has several interchangeable items at similar price points and preset bundles show weak take-up or high bounce.
ideas.do_not_run_when: The catalogue is small or the items are not interchangeable; the added configuration step is a real cost and has shown no metric movement in at least one reported case.
ideas.plain_english: Let shoppers build their own bundle instead of picking a preset.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when the catalogue has interchangeable items at similar prices and preset bundles show weak take up.

ideas.title: Third-party security seal at the buy or commit button
ideas.hypothesis: If a recognised security or trust seal is placed immediately beside the buy button rather than in the footer, then conversion will increase, because MECLABS reports a 13.2% gain in free-trial take-up from adding a Hacker Safe logo and a 5% lift from a trustmark under add-to-cart plus a persistent corner seal.
ideas.run_when: Site is unfamiliar to a large share of traffic, the product is high-consideration, or survey/session data shows payment-security anxiety.
ideas.do_not_run_when: Brand is already highly trusted in the category, or the seal is not one buyers recognise (an unknown badge adds noise, not reassurance).
ideas.plain_english: Put a recognised security seal right beside the buy button.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when the site is unfamiliar to much of its traffic or research shows payment security anxiety.

ideas.title: Abandoned-cart recovery email: existence, timing and whether it carries an incentive
ideas.hypothesis: If abandoners receive a fast recovery sequence and the later email carries a price incentive, then recovered revenue will increase, because MECLABS reports a first email at 1 hour converting 0.33% against 0.19% at 24 hours, and a 33% price reduction in the second email lifting email-to-sale 263% while still producing 133% more revenue than the undiscounted control.
ideas.run_when: Cart abandonment is measurable, email addresses are captured before the drop-off point, and margin can absorb an incentive on the later touch.
ideas.do_not_run_when: The discount would train the existing customer base to abandon deliberately, or the product is bought on a schedule where a 1-hour prompt reads as surveillance.
ideas.plain_english: Send a fast cart recovery email, with a discount on the follow up.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when abandonment is measurable, emails are captured before drop off, and margin can absorb a later incentive.

ideas.title: Star ratings and review counts on collection page product cards
ideas.hypothesis: If star ratings and review counts are shown on collection page product cards, then conversion rate will increase, because shoppers currently pick between visually similar products with no trust signal until they reach the PDP.
ideas.run_when: Reviews exist at product level but render only on the PDP, and the collection page shows many similar options.
ideas.do_not_run_when: Review coverage is thin, or ratings are low or wildly inconsistent across the grid.
ideas.plain_english: Show star ratings and review counts on collection page cards.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when reviews exist at product level but only render on the product page.

ideas.title: Subscription price shown alongside the one-time price on listing cards
ideas.hypothesis: If the subscription price is displayed next to the one-time price on product cards, then revenue per visitor will increase, because the subscription saving is currently only discoverable on the PDP.
ideas.run_when: A subscription offer exists with a real discount and listing cards show only a single or 'from' price.
ideas.do_not_run_when: There is no subscription programme, or the discount is small enough to read as noise.
ideas.plain_english: Show the subscription price next to the one time price on cards.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when a subscription offer with a real discount exists but cards show only a single price.

ideas.title: Subscription benefits shown without having to select the subscription option
ideas.hypothesis: If subscription benefits are expanded by default and written in specific brand language, then subscription orders per visitor will increase, because shoppers currently have to opt in before they can read what they get.
ideas.run_when: A subscription option exists but its benefits sit behind a radio button or a generic 'save 10%' line.
ideas.do_not_run_when: The subscription programme is unprofitable, or the benefit set is too thin to survive being read.
ideas.plain_english: Show what subscribers get without making them select it first.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when a subscription option exists but its benefits sit behind a radio button or a generic save line.

ideas.title: Cookie consent placement that does not block browsing
ideas.hypothesis: If the cookie consent banner is moved out of the way of the first screen instead of gating the site, then conversion rate will increase, because the interruption is currently the first thing every visitor has to resolve.
ideas.run_when: Consent is legally required and the current implementation blocks interaction until a choice is made.
ideas.do_not_run_when: Consent rate itself is the KPI for a campaign period, or local law requires a hard gate.
ideas.plain_english: Move the cookie banner so it stops blocking the first screen.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when consent is legally required and the current banner blocks interaction until a choice is made.

ideas.title: Filter groups collapsed by default instead of all expanded
ideas.hypothesis: If filter groups are collapsed by default, then conversion rate will increase, because a fully expanded filter panel pushes products down and makes the page feel like work.
ideas.run_when: The filter set is long and technical and analytics show low filter engagement relative to the screen space it takes.
ideas.do_not_run_when: Only one or two filters exist, or a single filter does almost all the work and must stay visible.
ideas.plain_english: Collapse the filter groups by default.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when the filter set is long and technical and engagement is low relative to the space it takes.

ideas.title: Price baked into the primary CTA button label
ideas.hypothesis: If the primary CTA label carries the exact price ('ADD TO CART - $99') instead of a bare action verb, then add-to-cart rate will rise, because two ConversionWise redesigns (McKays 'BUY NOW | $51.90', Beauvi 'ADD TO CART - £9.70') put commitment and cost on one control so the buyer does not have to look twice, and the library already treats price detail in a CTA label as its own lever (IC-002 installment microcopy on CTA).
ideas.run_when: Price sits visually apart from the button, or session replay shows repeated glance-back between button and price block; single-price SKUs where the number does not change with variant selection.
ideas.do_not_run_when: Price changes with variant, quantity or subscription toggle and the label cannot update reliably; high-ticket items where surfacing the number at the button is likely to suppress clicks you want reaching a finance or contact step; markets where tax-inclusive display rules make the button number ambiguous.
ideas.plain_english: Put the exact price inside the buy button label.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when price sits visually apart from the button and the SKU has one fixed price.

ideas.title: Order-level 'You Saved $X' row above the cart subtotal
ideas.hypothesis: If the cart totals block carries an explicit order-level 'You Saved $X' line immediately above Subtotal, then checkout-begin rate will rise, because all three ConversionWise cart-drawer redesigns (Nip+Fab, OSEA, candle brand) add exactly this row, making an already-earned discount visible at the moment the total is evaluated rather than leaving the buyer to infer it from struck-through line prices.
ideas.run_when: Discounts, tier promos or bundle pricing are already applied by the time the cart renders, and the current drawer shows only a subtotal; cart-abandon survey or replay shows price-shock at the totals block.
ideas.do_not_run_when: No discount is active for most sessions (an empty or $0 savings row reads as a missing deal and can suppress); the store is running a deliberate full-price positioning test (see IC-102); savings figure would be computed off an inflated list price you cannot defend.
ideas.plain_english: Add a you saved line above the cart subtotal.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when discounts are already applied by cart render and the drawer shows only a subtotal.

ideas.title: Proof claim or authority badge rendered onto the hero image
ideas.hypothesis: If the single strongest claim or third-party credential is composited onto the hero image itself rather than left as body copy or a separate badge section, then conversion rate will rise, because four ConversionWise redesigns place it there (Nip+Fab 'Clinically proven to decrease skin redness by 29% in 4 weeks', KittySpout '#1 Vet Recommended', Beauvi 'SheerLuxe Beauty Awards Winner 2022', Brian Curry 'Performing Artist Of The Year') so the proof is read passively by every visitor before any scroll, including the majority who never reach the proof sections.
ideas.run_when: There is one genuinely defensible claim (clinical result, category ranking, named award) and scroll data shows a large share of sessions never reaching the existing proof section; mobile, where the hero occupies the whole first viewport.
ideas.do_not_run_when: The claim needs an asterisk longer than the claim itself, or cannot survive a regulator or a competitor reading it; the hero image is the primary product-comprehension asset and an overlay would obscure the product (contrast with IC-119 and the OSEA floating-tab removal, where covering the hero lost); product photography is syndicated and cannot be re-composited per market.
ideas.plain_english: Put the strongest proof claim onto the hero image itself.
ideas.ideation_hint: Run when one defensible claim exists and scroll data shows most sessions never reach the proof section.

evidence.variant: Exposed quantity selector on the PDP, plus an iteration that defaulted the quantity to two
evidence.lift_note: Reported as 'up to +54% revenue per user for soap purchasers', i.e. a segment-scoped ceiling rather than a site-wide figure
evidence.context: Triggered by order data plus survey evidence that buyers already wanted multiple bars, so the change removed friction on an existing behaviour rather than manufacturing demand. Generalises to 'make the natural purchase quantity easy and salient' for consumables, but only prioritise after order-level data confirms multi-unit buying. Sample and significance not disclosed, so this must not outrank smaller statistically documented tests.

evidence.variant: Dedicated Shop Pay button in the cart drawer (a payment-icon treatment was also tested)
evidence.lift_note: Also +69.30% RPV, +19.33% checkout-start rate, +14.59% AOV
evidence.context: Positive movement on mobile and desktop and Fame rolled it out, but the published case discloses neither sample size nor statistical confidence, so the headline uplift must never rank above a smaller statistically documented result. Candidate conditions: standard Shopify cart-drawer architecture, high Shop Pay adoption in the audience, material cart abandonment.

evidence.variant: 'Upgrade to subscription and save 10%' control in the side cart
evidence.context: Consumable category with existing subscription economics. Experiment detail is weakly disclosed, and a subscription-only metric can hide deterioration elsewhere: total checkout CVR, immediate RPV, take rate, discount cost, retention and first-order margin all need tracking before this is called a win in a client programme.

evidence.variant: Full search field exposed in the header
evidence.lift_note: Also +12% RPV and +2% collection-page views
evidence.sample: Two weeks of runtime; visitor count not disclosed
evidence.context: Textbook research-to-hypothesis chain: only 0.76% of visitors used search, search users converted materially above average, and traffic was mostly mobile. But it reached only 80% significance after two weeks, below the 95% level the case itself cites, so it is directional rather than a confirmed winner. The reusable trigger is 'search users outperform average visitors while search utilisation is unusually low, particularly on mobile'.

evidence.variant: Sticky mobile filter and sort bar
evidence.lift_note: Filter/sort interaction increased 299.58%; RPV -1.8%; AOV flat; commercial measures did not reach significance
evidence.context: The canonical proof that engagement with the changed element is not a success metric. Usage of the control rose almost fourfold while every commercial measure moved slightly the wrong way and none reached significance. Blend classified it as a UX improvement, not a revenue result. Returning visitors showed some positive directional behaviour, which is not the same as a segment win.

evidence.variant: Image-supported mobile navigation
evidence.lift_note: Also RPV -4% and AOV -2% across all traffic
evidence.context: The all-traffic reading is the pre-planned result and it is negative on every commercial measure. Adding thumbnails to menu items cost conversion for this store; treat the pattern as carrying a negative prior until a client-specific reason to expect otherwise is on the table.

evidence.variant: Image-supported mobile navigation, traffic landing on one specific necklace PDP excluded
evidence.lift_note: Also RPV +4% and ATC +15% within the excluded-traffic segment
evidence.context: The exclusion was identified after looking at the data and no statistical confidence was reported, so this flips a loss into an apparent win purely by segment choice. Hypothesis-generating, never confirmatory: it earns a re-run with the segment pre-specified, not a place in the winners list.

evidence.variant: After a short delay, returning visitors with a non-empty persistent basket are shown a reminder that products remain in their basket, with a cart CTA
evidence.lift_note: 6 tests, 6 wins, 0 losses (100% win rate)
evidence.context: Highest replication count in the corpus and a 6/6 win rate. Published implementation is specifically mobile homepage. Requires persistent basket state and identifiable return visits; the delay before appearing is part of the treatment, and it must suppress for empty baskets. Caveat: all Evidoo tests come from one agency's (Valantic NL) client base, so 6 replications is not 6 independent research teams.

evidence.variant: Compact set of high-demand product categories exposed above the fold
evidence.lift_note: 25 tests, 60% wins, 8% losses (so roughly four in ten did not win, though outright losses were uncommon)
evidence.context: The 60% win rate matters more than the +5.1%. Good candidates: broad catalogue, several obvious high-volume categories, significant homepage entry traffic, category navigation already a material route. Poor candidates: single-product brands, very small catalogues, homepage traffic arriving from campaigns with one pre-defined intent. Single-agency source (Valantic NL).

evidence.industry: General consumer goods, electronics, fashion, furniture, pets, children's products, luxury, health/beauty, DIY
evidence.variant: Payment method labelled as carrying no charge, e.g. 'Visa - Free'
evidence.metric_label: average transaction KPI impact across 25 tests
evidence.lift_note: 25 mobile-checkout tests, 56% wins, 8% losses
evidence.context: Ranks high because replication strength compensates for how small the UI change is. Run only where customers could plausibly expect a payment fee and 'free' is factually correct for the labelled methods. Guardrail payment-method mix, payment failure and margin where payment costs vary. Single-agency source (Valantic NL).

evidence.variant: Hero image / category banner removed from the mobile product-overview page
evidence.lift_note: 17 tests, 58.9% wins, 5.8% losses
evidence.context: The principle is not 'hero banners are bad'. It applies where a decorative banner pushes products below the initial viewport without adding decision-critical information, so verify poor first-viewport product visibility before running. Worth laddering: remove the image but keep H1 and category copy, compact image/title treatment, or move supporting category content below the first products. Single-agency source (Valantic NL).

evidence.variant: Floating form labels
evidence.lift_note: 8 mobile tests, 0% win rate, 62.5% loss rate
evidence.context: Negative prior, not a prohibition: zero wins in eight mobile tests means any future floating-label variant needs strong client-specific evidence to overcome the historical record. The actionable inverse is the useful test for clients who already ship floating labels: restore persistent visible labels. Single-agency source (Valantic NL).

evidence.variant: Cart page with personalised free-shipping status: "Congratulations, you qualify for free shipping!" when over threshold, and "Just $17.45 more to qualify for free shipping" when under it. Reported alongside a companion variation that reduced distraction and clarified the page.
evidence.context: Mechanism is dynamic, personalised progress-to-threshold messaging replacing a static threshold statement in the cart. Threshold was $25 while average order value exceeded $100, so most shoppers were already qualified and the message read as confirmation rather than a spend prompt. The case reports the result as combining two variations (A: clarity and reduced distraction; B: value-proposition emphasis), so the 7.3% is not cleanly attributable to the personalised copy alone.

evidence.variant: Variation A reduced visual distraction and emphasised the Add to cart CTA; Variation B added that plus prominent "FREE SHIPPING on orders over $50" messaging on the product page.
evidence.context: Headline whole-test read before the team noticed the site had changed its free-shipping threshold from $50 to $75 on 29 July, mid-test. The flat aggregate hides two opposite effects, split out in the two rows below. Treat the aggregate as uninterpretable rather than as a null result.

evidence.variant: Product page carrying prominent "FREE SHIPPING on orders over $50" messaging (Variation B).
evidence.context: Threshold-split reanalysis. While the free-shipping threshold sat at $50, surfacing it on the PDP won. Site average order value was over $100, so a $50 threshold was comfortably clearable and the message read as a benefit already earned. This is the favourable half of the threshold reversal and it is a post-hoc segment, not the pre-planned read.

evidence.variant: Product page carrying prominent free-shipping-over-threshold messaging (Variation B), now stating the $75 threshold.
evidence.context: The reversal half of the same test. Once the threshold moved from $50 to $75 on 29 July, the same PDP free-shipping message went from a 6.56% gain to a 15% decrease. The identical change flipped sign purely on the threshold value, which is the transferable lesson: surfacing a shipping threshold on the PDP is only a win while the threshold reads as easy to clear against the site's AOV. Post-hoc segment analysis prompted by a mid-test merchandising change, not a pre-planned split.

evidence.variant: Free-shipping value proposition surfaced at different points of the funnel; variation set differed by device (Variation A on desktop, Variation C on mobile, Variation B reported for the aggregate).
evidence.lift_note: 3.74% increase in order confirmations with Variation B; the case also reports "Overall, there was a 2.9% order confirmation increase".
evidence.context: Iterative programme across the funnel run in two phases (May-June 2020, October-November 2020). The case's own framing is that the placement of the free-shipping message matters as much as the message itself, with different winning variations on desktop and mobile. No confidence, sample or per-variation detail published, so treat as directional.

evidence.variant: Light, conversational copy matching the brand's own voice.
evidence.context: Copy-only change on the first two funnel steps of a subscription sign-up. The case notes this is the class of small copy test that had previously been blocked internally, so the value is partly organisational. No confidence, sample or device data published.

evidence.variant: Products separated out individually with a bullet-point inventory of what is included.
evidence.context: Triggered by higher-than-expected pogosticking, showing users were navigating between pages to compare pricing across the bundle's components. Debundling removed that comparison trip. No confidence, sample or device data published.

evidence.variant: Variation A: added copy making the bundle discount explicit.
evidence.context: One arm of an A/B/C test iterating on the debundling winner. Stating the saving in words rather than leaving it implied in the prices. Small effect relative to the sibling arm below. No confidence or sample published.

evidence.variant: Variation B: add-on checkboxes deselected by default.
evidence.lift_note: Combined impact across both experiments reported as ">17% subscription conversion rate increase".
evidence.context: Runs the preselected-default idea in the opposite direction: removing the pre-tick raised subscription conversion. Useful counterweight to the default-selection doctrine, since the pre-tick was suppressing sign-up even though it raised items per order. The case reports the combined impact of the debundling and this A/B/C follow-up as more than a 17% subscription conversion rate increase. No confidence or sample published.

evidence.variant: Variation B: full-page stepped "configure your appliance" experience shown after proceed to checkout.
evidence.context: Two things change together: modal becomes a full-page stepped experience, and the moment moves from post-add-to-cart to post-proceed-to-checkout. The case reports the redesign as very effective on desktop but not as effective on mobile, where the full-page experience felt too similar to the control on a small screen. No confidence or sample published.

evidence.variant: Variation B: full-page stepped "configure your appliance" experience shown after proceed to checkout.
evidence.context: Second reported metric on the same Variation B. Paid delivery attachment moved almost as much as warranty attachment, so the effect is on the configure step as a whole rather than on one add-on category. No confidence or sample published.

evidence.variant: Variation A: full-page stepped "configure your appliance" experience shown after add to cart (same format change, earlier moment).
evidence.metric_label: orders with warranty or delivery attached
evidence.lift_note: No lift figure published for Variation A; described qualitatively as raising engagement and add-rates but not orders of the attached products.
evidence.context: The timing control arm. Variation A significantly reduced people ignoring or skipping past the modal and increased delivery and warranty adds, but did not move actual orders of those products. Isolates the timing variable: the same format placed after add to cart produced engagement without revenue, while placing it after proceed to checkout (Variation B) produced both. Attach-intent is not attach.

evidence.variant: Confirmation messaging reduced in size and framed as a completed step, with a prominent second step prompting "Add desserts, drinks, snacks & more from the Gousto Market".
evidence.context: Marketplace carries third-party products (wine, beer, desserts) and is high-margin, so ancillary sales were the deliberate target metric rather than a proxy. The mechanism is progress framing: marking the order as a completed step makes the add-on browse read as step two rather than an afterthought. The separately quoted 18x return on investment covers an 18-month expanded programme, not this test. No confidence, sample or duration published.

evidence.variant: Traditional collection page grid.
evidence.context: The editorialised layout was the incumbent and the plain grid was the challenger, so the win is for reverting to convention. Reads as a scannability and comparison result: the featured tile broke grid rhythm and cost revenue per user even though it looked more designed. One of the few SplitBase examples with both a confidence level and a sample size published.

evidence.variant: Side cart with a button to upgrade single products to a recurring order, framed as "upgrade to subscription & save 10%".
evidence.context: Places the subscription decision at the point intent is already confirmed rather than on the PDP where it competes with the buy decision itself. The stated 10% saving is part of the change, so the result is the offer and the placement together. Metric is subscription revenue specifically, not total revenue, so overall RPV impact is unreported. No confidence or sample published.

evidence.variant: Product comparison feature for the Hypervolt range, surfaced on collection and product pages.
evidence.lift_note: Reported duration "3 full weeks".
evidence.context: Research trigger was mobile users being unable to tell the Hypervolt models apart. Ran three full weeks. Multi-model range at similar price points with spec-level differences is the condition that makes comparison support pay. No confidence or sample published.

evidence.variant: Quantity field added to the product page with a default quantity of 2 soaps.
evidence.metric_label: revenue per user for soap purchasers
evidence.lift_note: Reported as "up to 54% in revenue per user for soap purchasers" - an upper bound on a purchaser segment, not a whole-test lift.
evidence.context: Two changes bundled: adding a quantity control at all, and defaulting it above one. Consumable low-price product where buying several is the normal behaviour, which is what makes the default defensible rather than a dark pattern. Result is quoted for a segment (soap purchasers), not all users, and as an upper bound, so treat as directional. The case's $800,000+ additional monthly revenue and $9.6M annualised figures are programme-level, not this test.

evidence.variant: More detailed landing page answering the questions customers commonly ask, in advertorial and long-form product formats.
evidence.lift_note: Reported as "increased conversion rates by over 43%" - a lower bound, no point estimate published.
evidence.context: Audience skews older and, per the brand's own survey and support-ticket research, prefers detailed product information. That audience characteristic is the condition, not a general rule that longer wins. Corroborated at the case-study page (https://splitbase.com/case-studies/laura-geller) which reports the same 43% figure at programme level.

evidence.variant: Colloquial, casual headline with a matching new CTA button.
evidence.context: Two variables move at once (headline tone and CTA button), so the headline effect is not isolated. Metric is clicks, an engagement proxy, with no downstream conversion or revenue read published, so a 124% click gain says nothing about order quality. Treat as a hook-strength signal only.

evidence.variant: Navigation with all items as plain text links, including Shop Bundles.
evidence.context: Counter-intuitive result reported as a surprise by the agency: de-emphasising the button raised its clicks, consistent with visual banner-blindness on a styled nav element. Click-only metric with no conversion or revenue read published, and the brand is unnamed, so evidence grade is low. Useful mainly as a caution against assuming button styling beats text in navigation.

evidence.variant: In-depth product details including a fabric information chart.
evidence.context: Structured spec data (a fabric chart) rather than more prose, on a category where material is a genuine purchase criterion. Brand unnamed and no confidence, sample or device published.

evidence.variant: Landing page headline taken verbatim from a customer quote.
evidence.lift_note: No lift percentage published; described only as "by far a winner".
evidence.context: Voice-of-customer headline beating internally written copy. Described as "by far a winner" with no figure published, so directional only.

evidence.variant: Build-your-own bundle builder tool.
evidence.metric_label: conversions, average order value and return on marketing spend
evidence.lift_note: No percentages published; reported as "greatly improved conversions, average order value, and overall return on marketing spend".
evidence.context: Catalogue of interchangeable personalised items at similar prices, which is the condition under which self-assembly beats presets. Pair with the row below, where removing a bundle builder at a different brand moved nothing: the tool is not a universal win.

evidence.variant: Bundle builder removed.
evidence.lift_note: No figures published; reported as "results showed no changes in any key metrics".
evidence.context: Removal test showing no change in any key metric, meaning the builder was earning nothing at this brand. Directly qualifies the Birthdate Co row above: the builder's value is brand-conditional and worth a removal test before investing in maintaining one. Brand unnamed and no figures published.

evidence.variant: Series of three GIFs on the product page demonstrating the application steps.
evidence.lift_note: The case reports a "26% conversion rate increase" at programme level (alongside a 6-figure monthly revenue boost); it is not published as this test's own lift.
evidence.context: Usability testing found social-sourced visitors would not read long descriptions, so the mechanism explanation had to be visual. Named in the case as the winning solution, but the 26% figure the case reports is a programme-level conversion rate increase across the engagement, not an isolated read on this change, so no lift is recorded against this row.

evidence.variant: "Highly Rated" badges applied to items with positive reviews
evidence.context: Review-derived badge on the product page lifted add-to-cart with a halo effect across inventory (product page views +0.27%). It did not move completed purchases, so the effect is early-funnel only.

evidence.variant: Consolidated single size filter surfaced above the fold
evidence.lift_note: Also reported as "+$12.7M incremental revenue impact"; size filter engagement +33.8%
evidence.context: Removed the wasted trip of clicking into a PDP only to find the size unavailable. Works where a hard-constraint attribute (size, fit, compatibility) disqualifies most of the catalogue for any one visitor.

evidence.variant: Visitor-specific personalised recommendations
evidence.context: Algorithmic personalisation beat a hand-picked static merchandising block on homepage traffic. Metric is a clickthrough proxy, not orders.

evidence.variant: Static bestseller recommendations shown to new visitors
evidence.context: Merchandising-logic swap with no design change: bestsellers act as social proof for cold first-time traffic.

evidence.variant: Wide variety of items across many categories ("full head-to-toe outfits")
evidence.lift_note: CTR also fell 10.4%
evidence.context: Breadth overwhelmed visitors. Loss-museum entry against the reflex of showing more categories on the homepage to serve everyone.

evidence.variant: Membership banner and unrelated elements removed
evidence.lift_note: "+$5.5M Incremental revenue" — no percentage disclosed
evidence.context: Distraction removal at the cart step, keeping visitors on the transaction rather than a secondary programme signup.

evidence.variant: Accepted credit card brands displayed prominently
evidence.lift_note: "+$2.7M Incremental revenue"; "5% of purchases shifted away from high-fee payment providers"
evidence.context: Payment-badge trust cue at checkout, with a margin side-effect: volume moved off high-fee providers.

evidence.variant: Multiple pricing and flow variants run as a multi-armed bandit
evidence.lift_note: AOV also up 8.4%
evidence.context: Add-on product priced and presented at checkout, with a bandit auto-routing traffic to winners rather than a fixed-horizon A/B call.

evidence.variant: Mini-cart with delete functionality plus enhancements (two variants)
evidence.lift_note: Mini-cart checkout clicks +7.89%
evidence.context: Results are reported only for "visitors who engaged with the mini-cart", a self-selected segment, so the headline overstates the sitewide effect.

evidence.variant: Zero-result searches redirected to machine-matched relevant product recommendations
evidence.lift_note: CTR +2.11%; "Annualized Net Measurable Value gain: $3.68M"
evidence.context: Dead-end recovery on internal site search. Effect scales with how much traffic actually hits a zero-results page.
