evidence.variant: Consistent promotional messaging for eligible items on both PLP and PDP
evidence.lift_note: Add to Cart rate +10.5%
evidence.context: Repeating the same eligibility signal across listing and product pages amplified it. The lever is consistency of the promo signal, not the promo itself.

evidence.variant: Descriptive badges overlaid on popular items ("Our Pick" tested against "Featured")
evidence.lift_note: Checkout clickthrough +1.3%; no significant effect on completed purchases
evidence.context: Wording mattered: "Our Pick" (brand endorsement) beat "Featured" (generic merchandising). Effect stopped at add-to-cart.

evidence.variant: Refill quantity selector added
evidence.context: Explicit quantity choice on a replenishment product raised both conversion and units per transaction.

evidence.variant: "Add to Bag" button above the product copy
evidence.lift_note: Add to Bag clicks +6%, purchase conversions +2%, Add to Wishlist clicks +19%
evidence.context: Pure reorder on the PDP: the buy control moved into the first viewport ahead of the descriptive copy.

evidence.variant: Countdown timer displayed
evidence.lift_note: Add to Bag clicks +4%
evidence.context: Urgency device on a menswear PDP tied to a real promotional deadline, not a manufactured one.

evidence.variant: Personalised leather bag customisation offer in the homepage block
evidence.lift_note: Homepage block clicks +210%, content snippet clicks +155%
evidence.context: A brand-anniversary banner replaced with a concrete offer the visitor can act on. The lever is offer-in-the-hero, not the anniversary.

evidence.variant: Contextual-bandit add-ons chosen on real-time conditions (weather, time of day)
evidence.context: Transfers to D2C: the checkout add-on changes with live context rather than being one fixed cross-sell for everyone.

evidence.variant: Geo-targeted sweepstakes popup shown only to users near the venue
evidence.lift_note: Overall personalised experience +8.1% against the non-personalised audience
evidence.context: Same popup, same offer, audience changed. The lift is an audience-definition result, not a creative one.

evidence.variant: Platinum (premium) tier repositioned to the left
evidence.lift_note: Add-ons +5.1%
evidence.context: Tier-ordering effect on a three-tier selector. Transfers directly to a D2C good-better-best bundle block.

evidence.variant: Prices shown directly on the options page
evidence.lift_note: "+£300k annual revenue"; step progression +0.55%
evidence.context: Price transparency moved earlier in the funnel. Small percentage, large absolute, because it applies to every visitor.

evidence.variant: Carousel slides plus short inline videos
evidence.lift_note: Exit rate -2%
evidence.context: Inline native video beat overlay video. Transfers to explaining an accessory or add-on on a PDP where text alone is doing the work.

evidence.variant: Message that short names do not mean short stories, with four extra pages added to the book, shown only to buyers entering 3-letter names
evidence.context: Objection-handling copy served to a narrow, self-identified segment (visitors from their largest paid channel). The objection was specific and real, not generic reassurance.

evidence.variant: Same short-name message targeted at both 3- and 4-letter names
evidence.lift_note: "showed no impact on conversion"
evidence.context: The first iteration diluted the segment and died. Narrowing the audience turned identical creative into the 18.1% win, which is the reusable lesson.

evidence.variant: All room types shown, including unavailable ones
evidence.lift_note: "€2.5 million in additional revenue while the test was running"
evidence.context: Showing unavailable inventory kept demand in the funnel instead of dead-ending it, and made the available options legible as a set. Rolled to 100%.

evidence.variant: Coupon code field moved to the first checkout step
evidence.lift_note: "€1.7 million in additional revenue during testing"
evidence.context: Placement variant of the coupon-field lever rather than removal: getting the discount question out of the way before the money moment. Rolled to 100%.

evidence.variant: 4 form fields
evidence.context: Illustrative entry in Optimizely's roundup with no brand, sample or confidence attached. Treat the magnitude as anecdote, the direction as consistent with the rest of the field-reduction record.

evidence.variant: Countdown clock added
evidence.context: Urgency applied to completing a multi-step signup. Headline summary only; the detail page is gone, so there is no control detail beyond this.

evidence.variant: Suggested donation amount of $60
evidence.lift_note: "didn't cost them a single donor, and it raised $200M"
evidence.context: Tripling the preset amount raised value with no drop in take-rate. Analogous to raising the recommended quantity or bundle default in D2C.

evidence.variant: CTA reading "start accessing your cash now"
evidence.context: Outcome-led CTA beat price/feature-led CTA. Headline summary only, no sample or confidence.

evidence.variant: Version C: product synopsis moved to the top of the page (tested against security seals, multi-device compatibility messaging, and speed-of-access emphasis)
evidence.lift_note: All four anxiety treatments beat control; C was the winner
evidence.context: Four-arm anxiety-mapping test. The biggest anxiety was not payment security but "will I actually want this", so answering the product-fit question first beat every trust treatment. Also covered at marketingexperiments.com/a-b-testing/testing-product-page-elements.

evidence.variant: Reinforcing headline copy, hero image, lighter colour scheme, shrunken "Why buy?" box, and a cart line confirming the FREE bonus offer
evidence.context: Five-day run. Maintained visual and emotional continuity from the pre-checkout pages and restated the promised bonus at the payment moment.

evidence.variant: Value proposition integrated into the checkout process
evidence.context: Roundup entry with the mechanism but no control detail: restating why-buy-from-us inside the checkout flow.

evidence.variant: Single vertical form, minimised fields, one "Book My Vacation" CTA
evidence.metric_label: conversion rate from billing information to confirmation
evidence.context: Collapsed a gated two-step form into one vertical flow with fewer fields. Multi-factor, so field count and gating are not separable.

evidence.variant: Secondary options demoted into product details behind a plus icon, single prominent "Checkout" CTA
evidence.context: Removed decision competition in the cart by ranking the options hierarchically instead of presenting three equal choices.

evidence.variant: Price order reversed so the lowest prices sat next to the CTA
evidence.context: Nothing about the prices changed, only their proximity to the action button. Read as price anxiety at the moment of the click.

evidence.variant: Primary benefit in the headline, benefits in the eye path, unrelated links moved to header/footer, tab content surfaced in a supporting column, CTA and price placed after the value presentation, credibility indicators next to the CTA
evidence.context: Ten-day run measured on actual sales, not add-to-carts, and beat both the control and a double control. Bundled rebuild, so no single element is isolated.

evidence.variant: Single primary CTA, product image as focal point, scannable description, left-nav value statements (Lifetime Guarantee, 100% Safe & Secure, Shop Confidently), BBB icon, one-step checkout
evidence.lift_note: The same 53.9% figure appears on marketingexperiments.com/conversion-marketing/radical-redesigns describing a similar automotive test; likely one experiment described twice
evidence.context: Bundled friction reduction, trust statements and a multi-step to one-step checkout collapse. Confounded: the checkout change cannot be separated from the page change.

evidence.brand: The Microbrewed Beer of the Month Club
evidence.variant: Single-step shopping cart plus a redesigned landing page adding owner imagery and personal copy
evidence.lift_note: Same test reports a 5.1% clickthrough lift and a 23.7% relative increase against post-holiday traffic
evidence.context: Six-step checkout collapsed to one page alongside owner-photo credibility elements, so step count and credibility move together.

evidence.variant: Simplified checkout with the forced registration and duplicate confirmation removed
evidence.lift_note: Body reads "over 68%"; the headline and URL say 67%. Recorded as 68 with the discrepancy noted
evidence.context: Forced account creation ahead of the order was the largest single removal, alongside a redundant second confirmation.

evidence.variant: Homepage rebuilt around the user's thought sequence with an explicit value proposition, plus the cart reduced from six steps to a single page
evidence.context: Confounded by design: homepage and cart changed together, so the 58% cannot be attributed to either. Useful as a ceiling for a full-funnel rebuild on a single-product store.

evidence.brand: undisclosed (financial software company selling to small businesses)
evidence.variant: Single-column layout with dropdown product selection, intro paragraph plus bullets, one strong product image, and a 60-day money-back guarantee
evidence.lift_note: The page also states "outperformed the control by 13%" and headlines 24% for the same winner; the three figures are never reconciled
evidence.context: Three treatments run. The winner removed competing products in favour of one product plus a variant selector, then added value copy and a guarantee.

evidence.variant: A single product with a dropdown to select the operating system
evidence.context: Collapsing three competing equal-weight products into one focal product with a variant selector. Clinic page: no confidence or sample disclosed.

evidence.variant: Treatment A: radio-button format for the product offers
evidence.context: On a multi-offer product page, a forced single-choice radio frame beat side-by-side comparison on page revenue. Note the comparison is treatment against treatment, not against the original page.

evidence.variant: Configurator letting visitors enter their own product criteria (tested against visual categories, text nav dropdown and visual nav dropdown)
evidence.lift_note: "outperformed the control and other treatments by a relative difference of 20%"
evidence.context: Four-treatment category page test. Replacing a browse-everything taxonomy with a criteria-entry step won; the other three treatments have no disclosed numbers.

evidence.variant: Product page with copy spelling out what the certification means for the buyer
evidence.lift_note: Source hedges: "increased conversion nearly 46%"
evidence.context: The win came from translating a certification badge into a consequence the buyer cares about (off-gassing, bedroom air quality), not from displaying the badge.

evidence.variant: Treatment #2: hero replaced with an actual photo of the home Fit Kit, three numbered process steps added, CTA changed to "Start Fit Profile"
evidence.lift_note: Headline states 72%
evidence.context: Real photo of the thing that arrives, plus an explicit three-step process and a specific CTA. Treatment #1 (image and steps, original CTA) has no disclosed number.

evidence.variant: Trustmark seal below Add to Cart plus a persistent scrolling trustmark in the lower screen corner
evidence.context: Third-party seal placed at the point of decision rather than the footer. Quoted by the brand in an interview, not a formal MECLABS writeup, so grade it low.

evidence.variant: Same offer page with the Hacker Safe logo added
evidence.context: Single-element test with nothing else changed, which is rare in this library and makes it the cleaner of the two seal results.

evidence.variant: Changed button colour and copy plus an inline email capture field
evidence.metric_label: clicks, free trials per unique visitor, free trials per clickthrough, paid subscriptions per unique visitor
evidence.lift_note: "30% fewer clicks", "13% more free trials per unique visitor", "61% more free trials per clickthrough", "24% more paid subscriptions per unique visitor"
evidence.context: A deliberate friction-add that qualified traffic: fewer clicks, better conversion all the way to paid. The standing argument against calling a test on a click proxy.

evidence.variant: Order form with online check added as a payment method, conversion rate 6.51%
evidence.context: Adding one payment option the audience actually used. One of very few MECLABS ecommerce tests with disclosed denominators.

evidence.variant: Checkout with steps removed
evidence.context: Roundup entry: step removal in checkout, no control detail beyond the mechanism.

evidence.variant: Accordion-style checkout
evidence.lift_note: Headline figure only; the page covers three experiments and does not attribute the 26% to one of them
evidence.context: Step consolidation into an accordion rather than separate pages. Weak sourcing, kept for direction only.

evidence.variant: Each requested data point justified with a reason it was needed
evidence.context: Field-level justification microcopy rather than field removal. The cheaper first move when a field cannot be deleted.

evidence.variant: Second recovery email carrying an incentive dropping the price from $29.00 to $19.95
evidence.lift_note: Conversion 0.19% to 0.69%; revenue per email $0.06 to $0.14, a stated 133% lift
evidence.context: A 33% price cut in the second recovery email more than paid for itself on net revenue. Note the very unequal arm sizes.

evidence.variant: Two-email recovery sequence sent 1 hour and 24 hours after abandonment
evidence.lift_note: First email 0.33%, second email 0.19%; "277 additional sales" and "$8,000" recovered revenue
evidence.context: Baseline economics for cart recovery. The 1-hour email beat the 24-hour one on rate, which argues for speed on the first touch.

evidence.brand: undisclosed ("Company X", recurring subscription with a free 30-day trial)
evidence.variant: Three-email automated sequence over 4 to 7 days, service-oriented rather than sales-pressure in tone
evidence.lift_note: Email 1: 1,226,841 sent, 1,428 sales, 0.116% email-to-sale, 3.754% click-to-sale. Email 2: 1,188,011 sent, 1,066 sales, 0.090%, 5.196%. Email 3: 1,145,661 sent, 1,583 sales, 0.138%, 6.783%. "Over six months, our test site generated an additional 4000+ sales"
evidence.sample: 3,560,513 messages sent across three emails over six months
evidence.context: Largest-sample recovery dataset here. Click-to-sale rises at every step of the sequence, so the later emails reach a smaller but far more committed audience.

evidence.variant: Link copy: "Open an Account"
evidence.lift_note: 18.95% of the "Open an Account" group reached application start vs 12.84% of "Learn More"
evidence.context: Single-factor CTA copy test carried all the way to funded accounts. Naming the commitment beat softening it, which transfers to add-to-cart and begin-checkout labels.

evidence.variant: Offer page stating "5,000 copies available" with soft urgency messaging: 768 DVDs, 0.115% conversion
evidence.context: Finite-supply framing on an offer page. The article itself warns this was a cluster test with several variables changed, so scarcity is not isolated.

evidence.variant: Free shipping on orders over $100
evidence.lift_note: "During the two weeks in which the free shipping was offered, the average order DROPPED to $154.70"
evidence.context: Threshold set below the existing AOV anchored customers down to it. The threshold has to sit above where baskets already land, not below.

evidence.brand: undisclosed health goods merchant (average order under $50)
evidence.variant: Free shipping on all orders over $250
evidence.metric_label: orders qualifying for the free shipping promotion
evidence.lift_note: "not a single sale qualified for free shipping" across the five weeks tested
evidence.context: Threshold at roughly 5x the average order produced zero take-up. The pair of results brackets the usable threshold range: above current AOV, within reach of it.

evidence.variant: $50 off coupon (roughly equivalent on the average $333 package, $250 minimum)
evidence.lift_note: "72% higher conversion rate" and "170% more revenue"
evidence.context: Economically near-identical offers framed differently. On a high-AOV basket the absolute figure read as the larger saving, and revenue moved further than conversion.

evidence.variant: Chance to win one of ten $50 Amazon gift cards (identical $500 total cost)
evidence.context: Cost-neutral prize restructure: a bigger prize at worse odds beat a smaller prize at better odds. Directly reusable in giveaway design.

evidence.variant: Bundle of conference plus professional training plus published materials at $2,005, framed as 33.5% off a $3,017 retail value, sold alongside a conference-only option at $1,505
evidence.lift_note: Also "45% more ticket sales" (400 vs 275)
evidence.sample: 275 tickets prior event; 400 tickets new event (159 conference-only, 241 bundle)
evidence.context: Year-over-year comparison, not a concurrent split, so treat the magnitude cautiously. The mechanism is offer architecture: raise the headline price and add an anchored bundle beside it.

evidence.variant: Four alternate price points: $50.00, $59.95, $75.00, $79.95
evidence.metric_label: paid subscriptions, conversion rate and total revenue
evidence.context: Price-elasticity ladder. The lowest price won on conversion rate and lost on revenue; the revenue-maximising point sat above the incumbent price, and revenue turned down again by $79.95.

evidence.lift_note: Three-day A/B/C table as recorded in control and variant fields
evidence.context: The mid price sold the most units, the highest price produced the most revenue, and the cheapest price lost on both. Cheapest is rarely the revenue answer.

evidence.variant: Strengthened headline, reorganised information, rewritten plan descriptions, quality-of-service claims, support details, guarantees and testimonials
evidence.metric_label: conversion rate and revenue per visit
evidence.lift_note: "128% more revenue per visit"
evidence.context: One-week A/B/C test. Mechanism given as friction reduction through clearer plan naming plus deliberate over-correction on anxiety with guarantees and proof.

evidence.variant: "Write in your own amount" field only, no suggested amounts
evidence.metric_label: conversion rate and revenue per donation
evidence.lift_note: "Control outperformed Treatment by 47.3% in conversion rate and 92.6% in revenue per donation"
evidence.context: Removing the anchors lost heavily on both rate and value. Pairs with the Optimizely $20 to $60 preset result: the preset does the deciding, so deleting it costs twice.

evidence.variant: Navigation de-emphasised and moved to the far right, left nav replaced with testimonials, primary objective in a bordered white box, larger CTA, competing section removed
evidence.lift_note: "conversions increased by more than 19%" — reported as a hedge, not a precise figure
evidence.context: Homepage focus test: navigation demoted, one objective promoted, social proof placed in the left-hand eye path.

evidence.variant: Multi-persona homepage with separate content paths, all still routing to the same target page
evidence.metric_label: clickthrough to the "find a treatment center" page
evidence.context: Counter-intuitive: adding segmented entry paths increased clickthrough to a single destination rather than diluting it, because each visitor found a route addressed to them.

evidence.variant: Treatment #3: two-column layout, concise value proposition with all value points above the fold, single primary CTA, free webinar registration offer, doubled featured-clients section
evidence.context: SaaS homepage, included because the mechanism (one objective, value points above the fold, more credibility early) is page-structure doctrine that transfers to a D2C homepage. All three treatments beat control.

evidence.variant: Ten headline variants; winner "Get Paid to Take FREE Surveys"
evidence.lift_note: "a statistically significant lift of 10.44%" for the winning headline; eight of the ten produced validated differences; the page title claims "nearly 29%" for the combined optimisation
evidence.context: Headline isolated from the form change. Winners led with the value point at the front of the headline; losers put it at the end.

evidence.variant: Explicit headline answering "what will I get", a statistical sub-headline, bullets moved higher on the page
evidence.lift_note: "doubled the conversion rate" — no percentage given
evidence.context: Value proposition moved into the headline for a seller with low brand recognition competing against known names. The author concedes elements were not isolated.

evidence.variant: Stacked highlighted feature and benefit bullets with supporting images, one CTA at the bottom, a time-limited incentive and a warning that premium data would be unavailable until upgrade
evidence.metric_label: conversions after the premium trial ends
evidence.lift_note: "almost 43%" relative difference
evidence.context: Upgrade offer at the paywall moment. Specific feature naming replaced vague "and more!" language, with a use-or-lose mechanic attached.

evidence.variant: Animated GIF demonstrating the product's movement
evidence.context: Motion conveyed a capability that static imagery and copy could not. Control described only as the pre-GIF version, so treat as directional.

evidence.variant: Two segmented versions, one promoting a traditional ecard and one a humorous ecard, split on lifecycle, past ecard-type history and sender behaviour
evidence.metric_label: conversions (site visits resulting in an ecard or subscription purchase)
evidence.context: Delivered by email but the lever is offer-by-purchase-history: same offer and send date, creative matched to what the customer bought before.

evidence.variant: Product-specific email alert button placed on product pages
evidence.lift_note: "318% revenue increase" and "53.3% conversion increase"
evidence.context: Capture moved from generic sitewide to product-level intent, so the resulting list was self-segmented by product and the send-back converted far harder.

evidence.variant: Treatment C, a product-page value proposition treatment
evidence.lift_note: Validated at 99% but the article's own conclusion is that this was a false positive
evidence.sample: 2-10 conversions/day; control had six consecutive days with zero conversions; observed test conversion 3.08% vs 3.83% historical
evidence.context: Kept deliberately as a methodology entry, not a mechanism one. The control underperformed its own historical rate on too few conversion events, and a follow-up A/A test on the same site had a cloned control beat an identical page by a relative 30%, which is the site's noise floor.

evidence.variant: Thumbnail images exposed in the PDP gallery
evidence.context: Session recordings and heatmaps showed mobile shoppers not viewing multiple product images, apparently unaware more existed. Also reported +3.44% checkout visits and +2.5% add to cart. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Sticky mobile add-to-cart with a secondary 'view product details' button
evidence.sample: extended test period, length not stated
evidence.context: Heatmaps and recordings showed mobile users scrolling down to reviews then back up to buy. Add-to-cart rate fell 20% while conversion rose, suggesting fewer but more committed adds. The case states the test did not reach statistical significance; it was implemented on the strength of a stable positive trend.

evidence.variant: Auto-ship information open by default plus explicit benefit messaging (Variant 2)
evidence.context: A/B/C test from UX competitor benchmarking. Variant 1 (open by default) also lifted metrics; Variant 2 (open plus benefit copy) won. Also reported +8.39% conversion rate and a 33.39% uplift the body calls revenue per visitor while the stat block labels it average order value for returning visitors, so treat that figure with caution. Add-to-cart rate dipped slightly. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Streamlined menu, subcategories moved to collection-page filters, no added imagery (Variant 1)
evidence.context: A/B/C/D test. Two imagery-led variants also beat control but the plain streamlined layout won, so the gain came from removing redundancy rather than from adding pictures. Also +3.62% conversion rate, +8% AOV, +5270% engagement with the navigation menu. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: 'Popular' badge next to the 4-week delivery option (Variant 1)
evidence.context: A/B/C on the highest-traffic PDP. The social-proof badge ('Popular', validated against 12 months of Recharge data) beat the authority badge ('Recommended' on 6 weeks), which moved purchase behaviour only marginally. Also +42.98% autoship selection, +28.95% RPV, +21.56% checkout visits. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Brand-based key value propositions below add-to-cart (Variant 1)
evidence.context: A/B/C run across the brand's UK and Ireland storefronts after a BFCM analysis showed reached-checkout rate falling. Brand-based KVPs beat product-based KVPs (+66.47% CVR) on the UK site. On the Ireland site both variants suppressed purchases and Blend reverted to control, so the same change was a loss in one market. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Same information consolidated into an accordion menu on the PDP
evidence.context: Competitor review showed rivals presenting the same detail in a single accordion block. Also +7.33% checkout visits, +6% add-to-cart clicks, +22% average session duration. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: 90-day return policy plus 1-year warranty below the add-to-cart CTA (Variant 1)
evidence.context: Triggered by support-contact search queries suggesting shoppers could not find basic policy information. The pairing beat the return policy alone: Variant 2 (90-day return only) lifted add-to-cart clicks 16.43% but cut conversion rate 16% and cart completion 19%, so the warranty appears to be the load-bearing half. Also +4.5% CVR, +5% cart completion. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Search bar exposed by default on mobile
evidence.context: Mobile-skewed traffic; searchers assumed to carry higher intent. Also +16.86% viewing search results, +8.63% clicks on add to bag, +33% clicks on the cart icon. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Price per dose, capsule, bar or serving displayed alongside the pack price
evidence.context: Prior user research showed unit price drove the purchase decision. Subscription CTA clicks rose 5.81%, which Blend reads as shoppers being more willing to commit long-term once the daily cost was explicit. Also +3.40% CVR, +23% add-to-cart clicks. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Add to Cart CTA recoloured to separate it from the secondary CTAs
evidence.context: Audit found no visual hierarchy among PDP CTAs. Also +8.14% add-to-cart clicks overall and, for new visitors, +66% add-to-cart clicks, +10% AOV, +16.40% average purchase revenue per user. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Description, Size and Ingredients presented as tabs (Variant 2)
evidence.context: A/B/C: basic accordion (Variant 1) versus tabs (Variant 2); tabs won, mainly for mobile navigation between sections. New visitors +23.56% RPV, returning visitors +13.19% add-to-cart rate, overall +11.17% CVR. The case states statistical significance only hovered around 70-80%; it was implemented on consistent segment trends.

evidence.variant: Search bar exposed on mobile devices
evidence.context: Search users converted 63% above site average in the audit. Headline metric on the page is profit per visitor +2.67%, which is outside this taxonomy, so RPV is recorded here. Also +2.3% CVR, +6% RPV for returning visitors, +0.8% subscription orders per visitor on mobile. Confidence recorded is the platform's 91% win probability, not a p-value; the platform also projected +682 orders per month and +2.9% monthly revenue.

evidence.variant: Search bar exposed by default across the site on mobile
evidence.context: Audit found search users converting 81% above site average. Cross-checked in Convert and GA4. Also +76% average purchase revenue per user, +38% clicks on search suggestions, +33% cart icon clicks; for new visitors +44% CVR and +14% AOV. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: USP section moved above the title and description (Variant 1)
evidence.context: Clarity heatmaps showed only 30% of users scrolled to the homepage USP section. A/B/C/D: USPs first won; USPs in the middle was competitive on desktop revenue (+251%); USPs alone with title and description removed underperformed, so surfacing the block beat stripping the rest. Also +66% average purchase revenue per user, +88% products per visitor, +56% add-to-cart clicks. No statistics disclosed and the lift is implausibly large for a homepage element, so treat it as directional.

evidence.variant: Radio buttons with the benefits of both options open by default
evidence.context: Audit hypothesis was that the green tabs read as CTAs, creating a false decision before the real one. Showing both option sets at once removed the misread and the click. Also +2.7% AOV, +27.9% RPV. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Express checkout options surfaced inside the cart
evidence.metric_label: Increase in Overall Revenue per Visitor
evidence.sample: sized off 90 days of Shopify Analytics
evidence.context: 90 days of payment data showed 30% Shopify Payments, 25% Google Pay, 16% PayPal, none of it visible before checkout. Mobile carried the win: +53.29% RPV and +16.46% CVR on mobile versus +6.79% CVR overall. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Selected reviews shown with customer imagery ahead of the rest of the reviews
evidence.context: Client-originated idea to draw attention to the review area. Also +5.02% add-to-cart clicks, +3.93% AOV, +7.73% average purchase revenue per user, +3.62% 50% scroll depth, +15.94% session duration. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Guarantee stated below the add-to-cart CTA
evidence.context: Headline figure is a desktop-only cut; the variant underperformed on mobile and was rolled out to desktop only. Click data showed low interaction, so mobile users read the element as a badge rather than a button. Also +20.03% revenue and +2% add-to-cart rate on desktop. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Consent banner at the bottom of the page, non-blocking (Variant 2, UK site)
evidence.context: A/B/C run separately across the brand's UK and Ireland sites. UK won with the bottom banner (+32% CVR, -22% bounce, +5% RPV); Ireland won with the top banner (+10.51% CVR, -9% bounce, +6% RPV), so placement did not transfer between markets. Blend notes the blocking original is still the right choice if consent rate is the KPI. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Full PDP redesign bundling image thumbnails, KVPs below add-to-cart, simplified benefits, an accordion for long-form content and a size guide
evidence.metric_label: increase in Conversion Rate for Desktop Devices
evidence.context: Deliberately a multi-change redesign, so it cannot attribute the win to any one element and Blend says so. Overall +10% CVR and +12% average purchase revenue per user; mobile +7% CVR and +11% APRU; desktop carried the headline. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Bulleted list of subscription benefits opened on the PDP
evidence.metric_label: Increase in Subscription Orders per Visitor
evidence.lift_note: Overall +17% subscription orders per visitor; desktop +32%, mobile +15%; subscription revenue per visitor +9%.
evidence.context: Headline on the page is the 32% desktop cut; the overall figure is +17% subscription orders per visitor, with mobile +15%. Overall conversion rate moved only 1%, so this shifted purchase mix rather than purchase rate. A concurrent promotional campaign was excluded from the read. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Shop Pay and Google Pay express buttons inside the Smart Cart
evidence.context: Chosen because most customers were already paying via express methods. Also +13% revenue, +12% average purchase revenue per user, +53% Shop Pay clicks, +40% Google Pay clicks, +60% Apple Pay clicks. The case states the test reached statistical significance but gives no figure.

evidence.variant: Logos replaced with a PayPal Express CTA in the Smart Cart
evidence.context: 26% of revenue already went through express checkout. This swapped a passive payment badge for an actionable express button, the same contrast Blend later ran at Fame. Also +35.60% AOV, +75.48% average purchase revenue per user. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Primary 'Order Now' plus secondary 'Discover Products' CTA
evidence.context: 80% of traffic was new visitors, so the hypothesis was that a hard buy CTA alone was too committal for first-timers. A/B/C: the softer 'Discover Products' alone lifted CVR 11.21% and RPV 12.44%; pairing primary and secondary CTAs beat it. Also +42.09% RPV, +6.03% checkout visits. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Message inside the gallery image above the fold linking to 'Explore Similar Products', anchored to the recommendation module
evidence.context: Recordings showed mobile users hitting a sold-out product and not scrolling, so both recovery routes were invisible. Also +8.48% clicks on 'Notify Me When Back in Stock' and +6.97% RPV, so the recovery link lifted the email capture rather than cannibalising it. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Exit-intent sign-up form offering a discount
evidence.context: Straight comparison of two exit-intent jobs: capture versus content redirect. Capture won. Also +2.9% CVR, +2% average purchase revenue per user, +37% pop-up CTA clicks, -3% pop-up close interactions. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Same module headed 'Rev up your cart'
evidence.context: Copy-only change to the default app heading, rewritten in the audience's own language. Also +12.91% CVR, +21.18% AOV. The case says results were 'approaching statistical significance' without giving a figure.

evidence.variant: Product recommendation module added to the cart
evidence.context: Heatmaps and recordings showed users still searching for products while on the cart page, so the cart was doing discovery work with no product surface. Also +7.46% CVR and +39% cart completion rate. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Search bar exposed on mobile
evidence.context: Headline figures are a returning-visitor cut found after the fact: GA4 showed returning visitors were 23% of visits but 43% of revenue, and they were the ones using search. Also +35% average purchase revenue per user and +46% revenue for that segment. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Banner on each site letting users switch to the sister brand
evidence.context: Cross-catalogue routing between two sites owned by the same client. Headline is the PerTronix figure; Aeromotive saw +28% CVR, +49% average purchase revenue per user and +0.88% collection page visits. PerTronix also +21.83% add-to-cart rate, +43% APRU. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Express payment buttons plus a '100% satisfaction guarantee' notice below the checkout CTA
evidence.context: Bundles express payment with a risk-reversal line, so the two effects cannot be separated. PayPal gained most engagement (+6.25% clicks) because Shop Pay was already visible on PDPs (+0.5% clicks). No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Brand-voice subscription line: 'Add more crunch with less cost'
evidence.context: Copy-only reframe of the same offer. Also +6% subscription rate and +13% AOV for returning visitors. The same brand-voice rewrite pattern won again in Jackson's Smart Cart upsell copy test. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Recommendation module moved above Applications, with Applications collapsed into an accordion (Variant 2)
evidence.context: Scroll maps showed the Applications block burying recommendations, but removing that content outright confused users who needed it. A/B/C: repositioning alone also won; repositioning plus accordion won bigger. Also +131.35% RPV, +12.87% add-to-cart rate. The case says significance was 'nearing 90%'.

evidence.variant: Add-to-cart only, express checkout removed
evidence.context: The inverse of Blend's usual express-checkout recommendation, and it won. Shopify and GA4 showed only 10% Apple Pay and 0.9% Google Pay usage, so the shortcut was pulling shoppers out of the journey for little benefit. Also +36.85% CVR, +3.57% add-to-cart clicks. Blend flags this explicitly as a case where the standard best practice did not hold.

evidence.variant: Thumbnail area activated plus a persistent sticky add-to-cart
evidence.context: Iteration on an earlier thumbnail test that won in the UK but failed in Ireland, where the thumbnails were thought to crowd the CTA on wider screens. Pairing thumbnails with a sticky CTA fixed it, so this is two changes at once. Also +9.61% add-to-cart clicks, +35.07% sticky CTA clicks, +6.26% RPV. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: '>' icons opening a separate drill-down menu panel
evidence.context: Recordings suggested misclicks caused by inline accordions obscuring the menu on small screens. Also +6.52% main category clicks, +5.83% subcategory clicks, +2.93% add-to-bag clicks, +6.72% RPV. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Star ratings and review counts on collection page product cards
evidence.metric_label: Increase in Average Order Value Overall
evidence.context: Audit found reviews were being collected but never shown at the browsing stage where the choice is actually made. Mobile carried it: +69.9% mobile CVR, +331.4% mobile RPV; overall +23.2% CVR and +113.7% RPV, with smaller desktop gains. The case states the test did not reach 95% significance; magnitudes this large on a low-volume high-ticket category should be treated as directional.

evidence.variant: Smart Cart upsell headed 'Add more crunch to your cart!'
evidence.metric_label: Increase in Product Additions in the Smart Cart
evidence.context: Came out of message mining: the default app copy carried no brand personality. Also +5% CVR, +5% cart completion rate, +6% clicks on proceed to checkout. The case says significance was reached quickly but gives no figure.

evidence.variant: Search bar exposed on mobile
evidence.context: Same pattern Blend ran across at least eight clients. Also +126% search trigger clicks, +109% average purchase revenue per user, +30% add to cart per session, +14% AOV. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Same content collapsed into an accordion beneath add-to-cart
evidence.context: Confidence recorded is the platform's 91.21% winning probability, not a p-value. Also +6% average purchase revenue per user, +2% AOV. Note the same accordion change lost overall on mobile for Vegepod, so device and consideration level condition this one.

evidence.variant: Simplified hero: bulleted value propositions, '4,000+ happy customers' proof line, clear primary and secondary CTAs
evidence.metric_label: Increase in Conversion Rate for Desktop Devices
evidence.context: Headline is a desktop cut. Mobile fell on both conversion rate and average purchase revenue per user, so the variant went live on desktop only. Also +27% desktop average purchase revenue per user and +8.27% add-to-cart rate. Several changes at once, so no single element is isolated. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: PDP content restructured into accordions
evidence.context: Overall the test lost: RPV -8%, conversion rate -2%, net revenue -12%. Mobile was badly negative (CVR -24%, RPV -28%) because high-consideration shoppers needed reassurance visible rather than one tap away. Desktop was strongly positive (+26% RPV, +15% CVR, +10% AOV, +51% checkout begin rate) and Blend recommended a desktop-only rollout. Recorded as inconclusive because the sitewide result is negative and the headline is a device cut. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: 'Back to Results' link on PDPs for users arriving from a collection or search results page
evidence.metric_label: increase in revenue per visitor (mobile only)
evidence.context: Only a subset of bucketed users ever saw the element, so the dashboard-level read understates it and the reported numbers come from a behaviour-defined audience. Mobile +5% RPV and +3% CVR with a 5.3% click-through on the link; desktop moved the other way (CVR -5%, RPV -1%). Rolled out on mobile only. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Persistent sticky add-to-cart bar on desktop
evidence.context: From user testing on a research-heavy category where shoppers read specs and install guides far down the page before deciding. Also +29.9% total revenue, +25% RPV, +18.69% products per visitor, +14.76% add-to-cart clicks, +6.3% AOV. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Sticky add-to-cart CTA on PDPs
evidence.context: Audit found some PDPs where only 8.74% of users ever reached the add-to-cart button. Also +26.31% average purchase revenue per user, +6.97% AOV, more checkout clicks and lower bounce rate. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Shop Pay, PayPal and Google Pay express buttons inside the cart drawer
evidence.context: Reasoning was that PDP-only express checkout caps the basket at one product. Moving it to the cart both sped up checkout and let baskets grow: +56.77% RPV and +38.89% average products per visitor alongside the conversion lift.

evidence.variant: Express checkout CTA directly below add-to-cart
evidence.context: Shopify Analytics showed Shop Pay was the most-used payment method but only visible at checkout, a visibility gap rather than a capability gap. Also +40.13% RPV, +3.19% AOV, +12.20% units per order and -24.23% abandoned checkout rate. Contrast with Jackson's and Stone Creek, where removing PDP express checkout won.

evidence.variant: Three specific trust propositions below add-to-cart: 'Chosen by over 20,000 families & 500+ funeral directors', 'Hundreds of deliveries per week to all 50 states', 'Rated 4.93/5 by thousands of families'
evidence.context: The propositions are specific and countable rather than generic reassurance, which is likely why they carried. Won on both devices, mobile hardest: mobile +47.7% add-to-cart, +32.7% CVR, +105.2% RPV, +54.6% AOV; desktop +19.9% ATC, +5.8% CVR, +10.9% RPV. Overall also +34.5% add-to-cart rate and +13.5% CVR. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: 'Shop by Roast' hyperlink near the top of the mobile PDP opening contextual roast guidance
evidence.context: Heatmaps showed only 2% of mobile users engaged with the 'Shop by Roast' section, so most were choosing without understanding the main product difference. The variant underperformed on desktop, where the same education was already reachable via navigation, and rolled out on mobile only. Also +5% RPV, +4% add-to-cart rate. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Tappable story-style widgets with lifestyle imagery linking to key categories
evidence.context: Session recordings showed mobile homepage visitors not travelling deeper. Basket value fell because the widgets sent shoppers to collection pages rather than product pages; Blend's stated follow-up was to route them straight to PDPs. Also +17.28% transactions per session, +19.3% cart completion rate. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Announcement bar in the mobile navigation linking to the subscription landing page
evidence.context: Also +24.77% visits to the subscription landing page, +16.58% checkout visits, +3.4% total revenue. AOV and RPV dipped slightly, which Blend attributes to the purchase mix shifting toward lower-value subscription orders. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: 'Shop All Coffee' CTA linking to collection pages
evidence.sample: low order volume, so results were deliberately not segmented
evidence.context: GA4 showed blog readers who reached collection pages were 25% more likely to purchase, while the on-page CTA sent them to a physical-location page. Also +34% view collection page rate, +32% add-to-cart rate, +15% begin checkout rate, +8% RPV. AOV fell 8% but conversion volume more than offset it. Blend avoided segmenting because order volume was low. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Best Sellers product module on the homepage
evidence.context: Recordings showed new visitors struggling to find products with no shop window on the homepage. Desktop strongest (+28% CVR, +23% RPV, +44% add-to-cart) with consistent positive mobile movement. Overall also +14.09% RPV, +21.18% add-to-cart rate, +3.16% view product page rate. AOV slipped 1.53%, which Blend treats as the normal signature of faster product discovery. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Visible colour swatches on desktop plus a bottom-positioned mobile sticky CTA (Variant 2)
evidence.context: A/B/C testing sticky CTA position (top versus bottom on mobile) alongside swatch visibility, so two changes move together. Conversion and add-to-cart rose (+7% CVR, +8% ATC, +27% sticky clicks) but revenue per visitor stayed level, and mobile RPV fell 18% while desktop conversion fell 5% despite +148% desktop sticky clicks. The case states device-level results did not reach significance and should be treated as directional. Recorded inconclusive: engagement up, revenue flat.

evidence.variant: All filters collapsed except the first
evidence.context: Extensive technical filter set that was necessary but consumed attention and screen space. Collapsing it raised filter clicks 235%, so hiding the controls made them more used, not less. Also +45.89% clicks on cart. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Payment method icons directly under add-to-cart, above the USPs (Variant 2)
evidence.context: A/B/C isolating placement: icons below the USPs (Variant 1) lost (-5% CVR, -4% RPV) while the same icons above the USPs won, so proximity to the CTA did the work. Also +9.08% RPV, +5% subscription orders per visitor, +3% AOV, with Intelligems projecting 67 additional orders per month. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Quick-select pill buttons for 2, 4, 6 and 8 weeks plus a 'More' dropdown for 1-10 weeks
evidence.context: Overall the variant lost: CVR -7%, RPV -13%, add-to-cart -5%, subscription orders per visitor -27%, subscription RPV -45%. Desktop was strongly positive (+31% CVR, +19% RPV, +14% ATC, an estimated 76 extra orders per month) and the change went live on desktop only. Headline is a device cut of a losing overall test. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Dynamic 'Save X% per oz' messaging on the 2 lb and 5 lb options (Variant 1)
evidence.context: A/B/C on a single product (Cream City Blend). Savings clarity alone beat savings clarity plus a 'Most popular!' badge on the 5 lb option, so the popularity cue added nothing here. Also +26% RPV, +117% subscription orders per visitor, +50% subscription RPV, +9% add-to-cart rate. AOV fell 10%, which Blend attributes to the mix shifting toward lower-value subscription orders. The case says the result reached statistical significance but gives no figure.

evidence.variant: Redesigned value proposition section with a clearer layout
evidence.context: An iteration on an element the client had already improved once, which is the pattern worth noting. Also +6.41% CVR, +8.35% add-to-cart rate, +48.33% subscription orders per visitor, +42.91% subscription RPV. The case says statistical significance was achieved but gives no figure.

evidence.variant: Full search bar exposed on desktop
evidence.context: Monthly reporting found desktop homepage entrants converting at 3.11% versus 4.20% on mobile, with the exposed mobile search bar the visible difference; searchers converted 137% above site average. Visits to PDPs and collection pages via search dipped slightly, which Blend reads as a shorter path rather than less engagement. Also +7.47% average purchase revenue per user, +13.9% checkout visits. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Search bar open and accessible on every page
evidence.context: Search users converted 54% above site average. Called after only one week on the strength of consistent lifts across several funnel stages plus prior wins on the same pattern, which is a short read. Also +9.93% RPV, +6.37% AOV, +3.35% add-to-cart rate, +4.4% checkout begin rate. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Full-width homepage imagery with a simplified layout (Variant 1)
evidence.context: A/B/C isolating visual treatment from routing: Variant 2 kept the control structure and only swapped the secondary CTA to Subscribe and Save, and it underperformed, so the gain came from the fuller-width imagery rather than the subscription route. Also +1% RPV and +1% profit per visitor, holding across devices. Subscription metrics fell, confounded by a Memorial Day promotion favouring one-time purchases and by the CTA pointing at a weaker subscription page. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Product-specific review on sound quality and performance placed high on the PDP (Variant 1)
evidence.context: Message mining found 75% of reviews positive, clustered on sound quality and ease of setup. The A/B/C isolates product-level from brand-level proof: the brand-trust review lifted add-to-cart 23.68% but cut conversion 7.38%, while the product-specific review converted. Also +10.77% RPV, +27.27% average products per visitor. Both variants slightly raised bounce rate. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Judge.me rotating review carousel added to PDPs
evidence.context: Iteration on an earlier win from surfacing reviews above the fold, extending a single review into a full carousel. Also +8.77% RPV, +7.41% average products per visitor, more add-to-cart and checkout progression, slightly lower bounce rate. Confidence recorded verbatim at 82%, below a conventional threshold.

evidence.variant: 'In-Stock Only' filter repositioned near the top of the filter options
evidence.context: Userfeel testing found shoppers struggling to find available parts. Run on two sister brands with opposite results: Aeromotive won (+8.04% add to cart, +19.71% checkout visits, -0.37% PDP visits, indicating shorter journeys) while PerTronix saw almost no change, which Blend attributes to PerTronix customers researching long-term builds rather than buying now. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Product-specific freshness copy: 'Batch Roasted to Order', 'Freshness Unlocked', 'Roast Date Printed Always', 'Same Day Shipping. Order by 1pm', 'Engineered for Freshness - Best Between Days 3-14' (Variant 2)
evidence.context: The A/B/C isolates copy, not placement: the corporate-flavoured banner ('Proudly a Certified B Corporation', 'Happiness Guaranteed') lost (-4% CVR and RPV, -19% subscription RPV) while product-specific freshness claims in the same slot won. Also +5% RPV, +18% subscription RPV, an estimated 31 extra monthly orders. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: 'User Photos' moved up beside the product images, with a more prominent 'See customer photos' CTA on desktop
evidence.context: Stat block reports 71.13% overall while the body text says 71.14%; both recorded here as written. Mobile +67.59% CVR, desktop +123.49% CVR, overall +24.40% RPV. Confidence recorded verbatim at 95%. Magnitudes are very large for a low-volume category, so treat as directional despite the stated significance.

evidence.variant: Pill-shaped subcategory text links above the fold (Variant B)
evidence.context: Homepage was 28% of sessions; heatmaps showed only 12% reaching Professional Advice and 6% reaching User Reviews. A/B/C isolating format: a story-style image module also won but the compact pills won bigger, so the space cost of the module mattered. Also +13.54% CVR, +10.05% add-to-cart rate. Subscription RPV fell 15.73%, concentrated among mobile and new visitors. Confidence recorded is the 83.1% probability of beating control, below 95%.

evidence.variant: Search bar implemented with Boost advanced search and typo correction
evidence.context: The hypothesis named returning visitors as the beneficiary and the result matched: returning visitors +28% CVR versus new visitors +5%. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Story widget format with an image per category (Variant 2)
evidence.context: A/B/C isolating format: text pills also beat control but image-led story widgets won. View PDP rate rose while view collection page rate fell, so shoppers routed straight to products rather than browsing categories. Consistent across desktop and mobile. Also +41% RPV, +37% checkout begin rate. The case says the test only approached statistical significance. Note the opposite format result at Wilson's Pet Food, where pills beat the image module.

evidence.variant: Sticky filter and sort bar available throughout scrolling
evidence.metric_label: increase in filter and sort clicks
evidence.context: Run in Intelligems with conversion rate as the stated primary goal, and it did not move: overall CVR -2.23%, RPV -1.80%, AOV flat. Returning visitors showed +2% product page views and +1% RPV and AOV, with a 93% probability of being best on returning-visitor product page views. Blend implemented it as a low-risk UX improvement and explicitly declined to claim a revenue win. Engagement up, revenue flat, so recorded inconclusive.

evidence.variant: Placeholder copy rewritten to prompt product search
evidence.context: A copy-only change to an already-visible search field, not a visibility change, so it sits inside the exposed-search idea as a second-order iteration. Also +4.53% subscription RPV, +2.26% subscription orders per visitor, +1% CVR, +1% AOV, with Intelligems projecting 313 additional orders per month. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Per-dose or per-capsule pricing with adjusted placement
evidence.context: A placement iteration after an earlier per-dose pricing test gave mixed results across regions. Also +2.75% autoship selection, +0.44% add-to-bag clicks. Revenue per visitor fell 0.55% and products per visitor 1.03%, which Blend attributes to the mix shifting toward subscription orders. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Action-and-object CTAs such as 'Shop Large Raised Garden Beds'
evidence.metric_label: Increase in View Product Page Rate
evidence.context: New visitors were 64% of traffic, and they responded hardest: +11% homepage CTA clicks and product page views, +26% RPV for that segment. Overall homepage CTA clicks +3.66%. Small sample. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Supporting image beside each key category link
evidence.context: The RPV gain came mainly through AOV (+24%) rather than conversion volume, with add-to-cart flat and product page view rate down 3%, which Blend reads as more precise self-selection rather than less engagement. Returning visitors strongest (+54% CVR, +66% RPV); new visitors +36% RPV. Also +14% CVR, +2% view collection page rate, with Intelligems projecting about 28 extra monthly orders. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Pump Finder pinned as a sticky CTA on mobile collection pages
evidence.context: Heatmaps showed mobile shoppers unable to identify the compatible pump. Average products per visitor fell 37.76%, which Blend treats as confirming the hypothesis: less uncertainty browsing, more decisive buying. Also +42.8% cart completion, +18.72% RPV, +13.4% AOV, +15.4% total revenue.

evidence.variant: Sticky pill-style subcategory carousel above the fold (Variant 2)
evidence.context: Only 29% of mobile users were reaching homepage subcategories. A/B/C isolating format: pills beat Instagram-style story circles, consistent with the Wilson's Pet Food result and opposite to Doctor Pooper's. Also +19.41% view collection rate, +9% RPV, with Intelligems projecting 75 extra orders per month. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Colour circles plus a variant name below that updates when a swatch is clicked (Variant 1)
evidence.context: Clarity heatmaps showed frequent swatch interaction without clear confirmation of what had been selected. A/B/C isolating a second change: adding extra spacing between swatches for mobile tapping (Variant 2) performed worse than naming alone, so confirmation beat tap-target size. Also +4.62% RPV, +4.85% subscription RPV, +1.12% add-to-cart rate, with Intelligems projecting about 1,959 extra orders per month. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Standard Checkout button plus a dedicated Shop Pay button matched to its height (Variant 2)
evidence.context: A/B/C in Intelligems isolating action from reassurance: passive payment icons (Variant 1) improved conversion, RPV and order value but cut checkout starts 7%, while the actionable Shop Pay button beat it on every overall measure. Also +69.30% RPV, +19.33% checkout begin rate, +14.59% AOV, with desktop moving most. Blend notes the test does not prove the mechanism. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Rebuy 'Recently Viewed Products' carousel above the best sellers module, hidden when there is no browsing history
evidence.context: Conditional display mattered: shoppers with no history saw no empty section. Also +13% eCommerce conversion rate and +2% subscription orders per visitor, with an estimated 159 additional orders per month. RPV was the stated primary KPI. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Colour swatches in a horizontal scroll (Variant 1)
evidence.context: A/B/C: open swatches beat both the dropdown and a hybrid text-plus-colour dropdown. Headline figures are the desktop-only cut, where it was published; overall subscription rate initially declined, which Blend attributes to shoppers exploring more options before committing, and improved once the variant was restricted to desktop. Also +3% CVR and +4% profit per visitor on desktop. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Featured customer review placed prominently near the key decision areas
evidence.context: Upstream actions moved against the win: add-to-cart rate fell slightly while conversion rose 7%, RPV 39% and AOV 29%, which Blend reads as the review making lower-intent shoppers more selective and the remainder more valuable. Desktop gained across every metric; mobile was mixed, with conversion and add-to-cart declining despite higher RPV and AOV. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Hero carrying both 'Shop by Vehicle' and 'Find a Fuel Pump' CTAs (Variant 2)
evidence.context: Conversion rate fell while RPV rose 6% and AOV 50%, so this bought intent quality rather than volume; Blend recommended rollout while watching order counts in busier traffic. A/B/C isolating CTA count: a single 'Shop by Vehicle' CTA (Variant 1) reduced both conversion rate and RPV, so one fitment route was distraction and two were useful. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Payment method logos displayed near the primary CTA (Variant 2)
evidence.context: The clean acceleration-versus-reassurance test on a high-ticket category, and reassurance won. Express checkout near the CTA (Variant 1) lost hard: RPV -25.55%, CVR -31.21%, add-to-cart -11.59%, which Blend attributes to shoppers wanting to review cart, shipping and pickup before committing on a grill. Payment logos left conversion roughly flat (-1.44%) but lifted AOV 31.67%, so the effect was on how much people spent, not how many bought. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Dynamic limited-time offer copy high on the PDP
evidence.context: Deliberately urgency without discounting, to avoid training price sensitivity or undercutting subscriptions. Note this was dynamic scarcity copy rather than a literal countdown timer. Also +15% RPV, +18% add-to-cart rate, with no reported harm to subscriptions. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Same banner moved above the collection section on mobile
evidence.context: Clarity heatmaps showed 70% of desktop users reaching the banner versus only 20% on mobile, with 60% of all traffic on mobile. A pure reposition, no copy change. Also +15.26% RPV, +12.41% cart icon clicks, +11.44% hamburger menu clicks, +3.91% PDP visits. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Visible image thumbnails below the main product image
evidence.context: Mobile was 92% of traffic and heatmaps showed repeated tapping on unlabelled variation circles. Add-to-cart rate and AOV stayed flat while conversion, RPV and checkout begin rose and abandonment fell, which Blend reads as more confident decisions rather than faster or bigger ones. New visitors +8% CVR and +10% RPV. Also +7.09% RPV and -4.46% abandoned checkout rate. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Approved payment icons (Shop Pay, Amazon Pay, Klarna, PayPal, cards) beneath the CTA (Variant 2)
evidence.metric_label: increase in mobile revenue per visitor
evidence.context: Combined result was negative. The express checkout arm underperformed on both devices (mobile CVR -14%, mobile RPV -21%) and payment icons reduced every major desktop metric. Only the mobile slice of the icons arm was positive (+1% CVR, +2% RPV, +1% AOV) and even there add-to-cart fell 1% and checkout begin 4%. Blend states significance was not supplied and the mobile result should stay directional; recommendation was mobile-only rollout of the icons.

evidence.variant: Rebuy Recently Viewed carousel near the fold on the homepage and further down on collection pages
evidence.context: Desktop carried it (+125.55% CVR, +459.23% revenue); mobile gained on AOV (+176.27%) and revenue (+133%) but conversion dipped 10.1%, which Blend attributes to the carousel consuming limited screen space. Overall +206.06% RPV and +191.8% AOV. Magnitudes are extreme for a 13-day test at 92% confidence, so treat as directional.

evidence.variant: All category images shown plus the original carousel split onto separate lines (Variant 2)
evidence.context: A/B/C isolating how much imagery: a partial treatment (featured category images with the original carousel) also beat control but the fuller visual menu won. Also +28% RPV, +8% AOV, +6% subscription RPV, with Intelligems projecting about 101 extra monthly orders. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Restructured navigation with images plus the brand's Trustpilot rating (Variant C)
evidence.context: Conversion moved 1% while RPV was -1% and AOV -1%, so this is a mid-funnel movement rather than a revenue win: add-to-cart +5% and checkout begin +6%. Blend calls the result directional rather than statistically conclusive. The images-only arm (Variant B) cut conversion 11%, so adding social proof to the menu was the lower-risk direction. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: 'Best Seller' badge on the top 10 products, 'New Arrival' on items uploaded in the last 30 days, and the 'Sale' badge replaced with an explicit percentage discount
evidence.context: Aimed at choice overwhelm across a wide urn and memorial range. Three badge changes at once, so no single cue is isolated. Also +10% add-to-cart rate, +3% RPV, +6% product page view rate, an estimated 23 extra monthly orders. The case states the test did not meet Blend's usual significance threshold, though product-level analysis showed uplift concentrated on the badged best sellers.

evidence.variant: Slightly smaller hero banner so the top of the product grid is immediately visible
evidence.context: Deliberately a small change to see how much a fold shift alone is worth. Desktop far stronger (+112.74% CVR, +196% RPV) than the overall figure; overall RPV +34.93%. Magnitudes are large for a banner resize on a low-volume category, so treat as directional. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Express checkout removed from the PDP, routing shoppers through the cart
evidence.context: Second Blend case where removing PDP express checkout won, alongside Jackson's. The reasoning is that the shortcut skips the cart, and with it the upsell surface. Also +20% RPV, +6.29% AOV, +10% add-to-cart rate. Subscription orders per visitor fell 7.21% while subscription revenue rose 3.35%. Confidence recorded verbatim at 86%.

evidence.variant: Persistent sticky Add to Cart CTA (Variant 1)
evidence.context: A/B/C isolating what the sticky CTA should say: a sticky 10% Subscribe & Save CTA in the same position also won (+28.56% CVR, +31.36% RPV) but lost to the plain add-to-cart, which Blend attributes to subscription adding a second decision. Also +48.28% RPV, +47.10% average products per visitor, and slightly lower bounce rate. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Sticky filter and sort bar always visible on mobile collection pages
evidence.context: Same change as the Little Bible Stories test and the opposite outcome, so the conditioning factor looks like catalogue value spread: on a high-ticket range with real specification differences, easier filtering moved shoppers toward better-suited, more expensive products (AOV +60.66%). Also +21.39% CVR, +34.01% add-to-cart rate, +10.45% filter and sort clicks, +2.02% view product page rate. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: A positive, product-specific customer review positioned near the top of the page
evidence.context: Heatmaps showed very few shoppers reaching the review section. Small but consistent lifts across the funnel: +1.34% CVR, +2% add-to-cart rate, +2.5% AOV, +1.32% subscription RPV. Blend reads the AOV movement as trust affecting willingness to spend, not just willingness to buy. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Dynamic 'Subscribe & Save X%' primary CTA pulling the live discount from Skio
evidence.context: Puts the exact saving in the button rather than asking shoppers to process the pricing structure first. Also +13% RPV, +9% subscription RPV, +3% AOV, with Intelligems estimating 95 extra monthly orders. Subscription order volume dipped 10% even as revenue rose, so the win came from simplifying the primary decision rather than from more subscriptions. No statistics disclosed. Note the opposite framing lost at Jackson's, where a sticky Subscribe & Save CTA underperformed a plain add-to-cart.

evidence.variant: Both the one-time price and the subscription price shown on the product card (Variant 2)
evidence.context: A/B/C isolating anchor versus comparison: showing only the subscription price as the 'From' price (Variant 1) drove more subscription behaviour (+22% subscription orders per visitor, +40% subscription RPV) but the dual display delivered the stronger overall revenue result. Variant 2 also +2% CVR, +4% AOV, +17% subscription orders per visitor, +14% subscription RPV. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Coffees grouped by flavour profile: Bright, Balanced, Bold (Variant 1)
evidence.context: A/B/C isolating explanatory copy: adding descriptive copy under the same flavour subcategories (Variant 2) lifted subscription RPV 44% and AOV 14% but hurt overall purchasing, so the labels carried the win and the extra copy cost more than it gave. Variant 1 also +2% CVR, +9% AOV, +2% product page view rate, +3% collection page view rate. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Circular category icons in the navigation (Variant 1)
evidence.context: Headline figures are the mobile cut; both variants reduced conversion and RPV on desktop, where the hover menu was already efficient, so it went live on mobile only. Mobile: circles +385% subscription RPV, +11% CVR, +12% RPV; pills +201% subscription RPV, +9% CVR, +8% RPV. The subscription magnitudes are extreme and no statistics are disclosed, so treat as directional.

evidence.variant: Pill-style subcategory widgets on collection pages (Variant 2)
evidence.context: A/B/C isolating format: Instagram-style cards also won (+2.56% CVR, +3.02% RPV) but pills won bigger, projected at 614 extra monthly orders against 286. Blend's stated theory is that shoppers arriving from a PDP mistook the card format for a shoppable story they had already seen. Variant 2 also +5.88% RPV, +14.95% subscription orders per visitor, +16.73% subscription RPV. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Sub-category widgets placed directly above the product grid
evidence.context: Conversion rate fell 24.13% while RPV rose 31.77% and add-to-cart 7.65%, so this is a revenue-over-conversion call that Blend made explicitly on the grounds that broader exploration raised revenue per session. Worth treating as a genuinely split result rather than a clean win. No statistics disclosed.

evidence.variant: Search field displayed by default, with reduced header height and tighter spacing to limit fold cost
evidence.sample: two-week A/B test on mobile, run in Intelligems
evidence.context: Only 0.76% of shoppers used search despite searchers converting 50% above site average, with 76% of traffic on mobile. The variant also shrank the header so the new field did not simply push content down. Also +12% RPV, +2% view collection page rate, small add-to-cart gain; AOV -1% and product page view rate -2%. Confidence recorded verbatim at 80%, which Blend flags as below the usual 95% threshold. The audit also found 4% of searches returning no results, named as the follow-up test.

evidence.variant: Image-led category tiles for bags and accessories plus direct links to information pages
evidence.context: The full-period read showed a 2% conversion-rate decrease and overlapped a high-demand product launch and pre-order period. The reported figures come from a re-analysis excluding visits to the promoted product page: +13% RPV, +11% AOV, +2% CVR, +6% checkout begin rate, with product page view rate down 1%. Blend states the result had not reached significance and is treating it as directional until a representative sample lands.

evidence.variant: Approved product imagery added beside category and subcategory links
evidence.metric_label: increase in conversion rate in exclusion analysis
evidence.context: Across all traffic the variant lost: conversion rate -2%, RPV -4%, AOV -2%, collection page views -3%. An exclusion analysis identified visitors landing on the Bar Cremation Necklace product page as driving the decline; removing them produced +20% CVR, +15% add-to-cart rate, +4% RPV, but collection page views still fell 4%. Blend states statistical confidence was not reported and the exclusion was identified after reviewing the data, so the interpretation is not proven. Rolled out selectively on urn subcategory menus only. 78% of visitors were first-time.

evidence.variant: Descriptive text labels added alongside each icon
evidence.context: Returning visitors responded hardest (+12.5% CVR, +16.56% RPV), new visitors +9.58% CVR, overall +2.95% RPV. No statistics disclosed.
